In summary, the documented role of (±)-2-Amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (AP5) in angiogenesis and cancer metastasis is based on its function as a competitive NMDA receptor antagonist. Its key anti-angiogenic mechanisms involve blocking glutamate signaling on endothelial cells, thereby directly inhibiting endothelial cell tube formation and migration (Patent WO2017093354A1, bioRxiv 10.1101/134924). In the context of cancer metastasis, AP5 can directly reduce tumor cell proliferation by inducing cell cycle arrest (reviewed in IJMS 2023), disrupt pro-metastatic neuron-cancer synaptic communication (Cancer Cell 2025), and enhance the efficacy of anti-cancer drugs by downregulating MDR transporters (PMC5788303).

# Documented Role of AIDA in Angiogenesis or Cancer Metastasis

## Summary Finding

**AIDA (1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid) has no documented direct role in angiogenesis or cancer metastasis in the peer-reviewed literature.** In the single study where it was tested in a cancer context, it was explicitly reported to have **no effect** on tumor cell proliferation. The broader literature does, however, validate its target, mGluR1, as a mediator of angiogenesis and tumor progression, though this work was performed using other, more potent mGluR1 antagonists.

---

## Evidence for the Absence of a Direct Anti-Cancer Role

### Negative Result in Melanoma Cell Proliferation

The only peer-reviewed cancer study that directly tested AIDA reported that it failed to inhibit the growth of human melanoma cell lines:

> **Haas HS, Pfragner R, Siegl V, Ingolic E, Heintz E, Schraml E, Schauenstein K.** "The non-competitive metabotropic glutamate receptor-1 antagonist CPCCOEt inhibits the in vitro growth of human melanoma." *Oncology Reports*, 2007, 17(6): 1399–1404.

In this study, the authors tested both the non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist CPCCOEt and the competitive antagonist AIDA on two human melanoma cell lines (HBMC and n15006). They reported:

> "Interestingly, the competitive mGluR1 antagonist (RS)-1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid (**AIDA**), as well as the agonists (1S,3R-)1-aminocyclopentane-1,3-dicarboxylic acid (ACPD) and glutamate per se **did not affect cell proliferation of both cell lines**."

In contrast, the non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist CPCCOEt significantly inhibited melanoma cell growth in a dose-dependent manner. No angiogenesis or metastasis-specific endpoints were assessed for AIDA in this or any subsequent study.

---

## Pharmacological Characterization of AIDA (Background Context)

AIDA was first described and characterized as a competitive antagonist at group I metabotropic glutamate receptors (specifically mGluR1/mGluR1a) in neuronal systems:

- **Pellicciari R, Luneia R, Costantino G, Marinozzi M, Natalini B, Jakobsen P, Kanstrup A, Lombardi G, Moroni F, Thomsen C.** "1-Aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid: A novel antagonist at phospholipase C-linked metabotropic glutamate receptors." *Journal of Medicinal Chemistry*, 1995, 38(19): 3717–3719. **DOI:** [10.1021/jm00019a002](https://doi.org/10.1021/jm00019a002)

- **Moroni F, Lombardi G, Thomsen C, Leonardi P, Attucci S, Peruginelli F, Torregrossa SA, Pellegrini-Giampietro DE, Luneia R, Pellicciari R.** "Pharmacological characterization of 1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid, a potent mGluR1 antagonist." *Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics*, 1997, 281(2): 721–729. **PMID:** 9152378.

AIDA acts as a **competitive (orthosteric) antagonist** at the glutamate-binding site of mGluR1, blocking phospholipase C (PLC) activation and downstream IP3/DAG signaling. It shows selectivity for group I mGluRs over group II and III receptors and has no activity at ionotropic glutamate receptors. This pharmacological profile has made it a useful tool compound in neuroscience (particularly in cerebral ischemia models), but it has not been translated into cancer research.

---

## The Validated Target: mGluR1 in Angiogenesis and Cancer

Although AIDA itself has no documented anti-angiogenic or anti-metastatic role, its molecular target (mGluR1) has been extensively validated as a mediator of angiogenesis and tumor progression when inhibited by *other* pharmacological agents or genetic silencing:

### 1. mGluR1 in Tumor Angiogenesis (Breast Cancer)

> **Speyer CL, Hachem AH, Assi AA, Johnson JS, DeVries JA, Gorski DH.** "Metabotropic glutamate receptor-1 as a novel target for the antiangiogenic treatment of breast cancer." *PLoS ONE*, 2014, 9(3): e88830. **DOI:** [10.1371/journal.pone.0088830](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0088830)

Key mechanistic findings:
- mGluR1 was detected in human endothelial cells (HUVEC, HMEC-1, HDEC, HLEC)
- mGluR1-specific inhibitors (BAY36-7620, YM298198) and shRNA silencing suppressed endothelial cell proliferation
- BAY36-7620 inhibited Matrigel tube formation by up to 98% in HUVECs
- Loss of mGluR1 activity reduced angiogenesis in murine Matrigel sponge and tumor models
- mGluR1 was proposed to play a **dual role** in triple-negative breast cancer: direct stimulation of tumor cell growth and promotion of tumor angiogenesis via downstream MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR/HIF-1α pathways

### 2. mGluR1 in Metastasis and Tumor Progression

> **Xie L, Zhang L, Hu K, Hanyu M, Zhang Y, Fujinaga M, et al.** "A ²¹¹At-labelled mGluR1 inhibitor induces cancer senescence to elicit long-lasting anti-tumor efficacy." *Cell Reports Medicine*, 2023, 4(4): 100960. **DOI:** [10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.100960](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2023.100960)

This study demonstrated that mGluR1 is frequently overexpressed across 32 tumor types and that targeting mGluR1 with a radiopharmaceutical:
- Downregulated mGluR1 oncoprotein expression
- Decreased pro-angiogenic *VEGFA* and pro-metastatic *MET* gene expression
- Suppressed tumor angiogenesis (reduced CD31-positive vessels)
- Reprogrammed the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) into "angiogenesis-antagonizing and metastasis-antagonizing" variants
- Achieved complete tumor regression in ~50% of mGluR1⁺ breast and pancreatic cancer models

Mechanistic pathways implicated: mGluR1 signals through MAPK, PI3K/AKT, and AKT/mTOR/HIF-1 pathways to promote tumor growth, angiogenesis, and metastasis.

### 3. mGluR1 Regulation of Inflammation in the Tumor Microenvironment

> **Sexton RE, Hachem AH, Assi AA, et al.** "Metabotropic glutamate receptor-1 regulates inflammation in triple negative breast cancer." *Scientific Reports*, 2018, 8: 16008. **DOI:** [10.1038/s41598-018-34502-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-34502-8)

This study showed that mGluR1 acts as a negative regulator of inflammatory chemokine production (CXCL1, IL-8) and neutrophil transmigration in TNBC, adding an additional dimension to its role in shaping the tumor microenvironment relevant to metastasis.

---

## Mechanistic Rationale: Why AIDA May Have Been Ineffective

The discrepancy between AIDA's lack of anti-cancer activity and the efficacy of non-competitive mGluR1 antagonists (CPCCOEt, BAY36-7620, JNJ16259685) may be explained by pharmacological differences:

1. **Competitive vs. non-competitive antagonism**: AIDA is a competitive (orthosteric) antagonist that competes directly with glutamate at the ligand-binding site. In the tumor microenvironment, where melanoma and breast cancer cells release high concentrations of glutamate (creating an autocrine/paracrine loop), competitive antagonists like AIDA may be outcompeted by the high local glutamate concentration. Non-competitive (allosteric) antagonists like CPCCOEt and BAY36-7620 bind to a topographically distinct site within the transmembrane domain and are not surmountable by excess ligand.

2. **Potency**: AIDA has relatively modest potency (IC₅₀ in the micromolar range for mGluR1 inhibition) compared to more modern non-competitive antagonists.

3. **Study scope**: Only one cancer-relevant study tested AIDA, and only in a cell proliferation context. No dedicated angiogenesis assays (tube formation, in vivo Matrigel plug, etc.) or metastasis assays were performed with AIDA specifically.

---

## Conclusion

**There is no documented role for AIDA in angiogenesis or cancer metastasis.** In the single cancer study where it was evaluated, AIDA failed to inhibit melanoma cell proliferation. The absence of evidence should not be conflated with evidence of absence—no dedicated angiogenesis or metastasis studies using AIDA have been published. The broader mGluR1 literature demonstrates that alternative, non-competitive antagonists of this receptor (BAY36-7620, CPCCOEt, JNJ16259685, and riluzole) exhibit clear anti-angiogenic and anti-tumor activities in breast cancer and melanoma models, suggesting AIDA's lack of activity may reflect its pharmacological limitations (competitive antagonism, modest potency) rather than target invalidity.

# Documented Role of AIDA in Angiogenesis or Cancer Metastasis

## Bottom Line: No documented role exists for AIDA in angiogenesis or cancer metastasis.

After an exhaustive literature search, **AIDA (1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid; UPF-523) has no demonstrated role in angiogenesis or cancer metastasis in the peer-reviewed literature.** The sole cancer-relevant study that directly tested AIDA reported a **negative result** — it had no effect on tumor cell proliferation.

---

## What Is AIDA?

AIDA is a **competitive antagonist of group I metabotropic glutamate receptors**, specifically mGluR1 (mGlu1a), with an IC₅₀ of 214 μM. It is inactive at group II (mGlu2), group III (mGlu4), and ionotropic glutamate receptors. It is centrally active following systemic administration.

- **Key characterization paper:**
  > Moroni F, Lombardi G, Thomsen C, Leonardi P, Attucci S, Peruginelli F, Torregrossa SA, Pellegrini-Giampietro DE, Luneia R, Pellicciari R. "Pharmacological characterization of 1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid, a potent mGluR1 antagonist." *Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics*, 1997, 281(2): 721–729. PMID: 9152378.

---

## The Critical Distinction: mGluR1 vs. AIDA

It is essential to distinguish between the *target* (mGluR1) and the *drug* (AIDA):

### mGluR1 IS implicated in cancer angiogenesis and metastasis

Multiple high-quality studies have established that mGluR1 promotes tumor progression, angiogenesis, and metastasis. However, **none of these studies used AIDA** as the pharmacological probe. The mGluR1 inhibitors employed in cancer/angiogenesis research include:

- **BAY36-7620** (non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist/inverse agonist)
- **Riluzole** (glutamate release inhibitor with indirect mGluR1 effects)
- **LY367385** (competitive mGluR1 antagonist)
- **CPCCOEt** (non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist)
- **YM298198** (non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist)
- **JNJ16259685** (selective non-competitive mGluR1 antagonist)

Key mGluR1–angiogenesis paper (did NOT use AIDA):

> Speyer CL, Hachem AH, Assi AA, Johnson JS, DeVries JA, Gorski DH. "Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor-1 as a Novel Target for the Antiangiogenic Treatment of Breast Cancer." *PLoS ONE*, 2014, 9(3): e88830. DOI: [10.1371/journal.pone.0088830](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0088830).

### AIDA itself has NO demonstrated role

The only peer-reviewed cancer study that directly tested AIDA found it **ineffective**:

> Haas HS, Pfragner R, Siegl V, Ingolic E, Heintz E, Schraml E, Schauenstein K. "The non-competitive metabotropic glutamate receptor-1 antagonist CPCCOEt inhibits the in vitro growth of human melanoma." *Oncology Reports*, 2007, 17(6): 1399–1404. DOI: [10.3892/or.17.6.1399](https://doi.org/10.3892/or.17.6.1399).

In this study, the authors explicitly stated: *"Interestingly, the competitive mGluR1 antagonist (RS)-1-aminoindan-1,5-dicarboxylic acid (AIDA), as well as the agonists (1S,3R-)1-aminocyclopentane-1,3-dicarboxylic acid (ACPD) and glutamate per se did not affect cell proliferation of both cell lines."* This was in contrast to CPCCOEt, which significantly and dose-dependently inhibited the growth of both human melanoma cell lines tested (HBMC and n15006).

---

## Why Might AIDA Lack Anti-Cancer Activity?

Several pharmacological factors likely explain the discrepancy:

1. **Competitive vs. non-competitive mechanism**: AIDA is an orthosteric (competitive) antagonist, meaning it competes with glutamate at the ligand-binding site. In the tumor microenvironment, where extracellular glutamate levels are often markedly elevated (as shown in melanoma, glioma, and breast cancer), high ambient glutamate may outcompete AIDA. In contrast, CPCCOEt, BAY36-7620, and JNJ16259685 are non-competitive (allosteric) antagonists that bind to transmembrane domains and can inhibit both agonist-induced and constitutive receptor activity regardless of glutamate concentration.

2. **Relatively low potency**: AIDA's IC₅₀ of 214 μM is considerably weaker than more modern mGluR1 antagonists.

3. **Constitutive activity**: mGluR1 exhibits constitutive (ligand-independent) activity when overexpressed in cancer cells. Non-competitive antagonists with inverse agonist activity (e.g., BAY36-7620) can suppress this constitutive signaling, whereas competitive antagonists like AIDA generally cannot.

---

## Other Contexts Where AIDA Has Been Used (Non-Cancer)

For completeness, AIDA has been employed as an mGluR1 antagonist in:

- **Cerebral ischemia/neuroprotection** — e.g., Pellegrini-Giampietro et al., *European Journal of Neuroscience*, 1999
- **Brain endothelial cell protection from oxidative stress** — e.g., Lin & Maiese, *Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism*, 2001 (DOI: [10.1097/00004647-200103000-00010](https://doi.org/10.1097/00004647-200103000-00010)) — where AIDA did *not* protect against NO-induced DNA fragmentation
- **Neurovascular coupling** — e.g., Shi et al., *Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow & Metabolism*, 2008 — used at 100 μM to study whisker-stimulation-evoked blood flow responses
- **Epilepsy/anticonvulsant studies**

None of these studies address tumor angiogenesis or cancer metastasis.

---

## Summary

| Aspect | Finding |
|---|---|
| **AIDA in cancer angiogenesis** | No documented role |
| **AIDA in cancer metastasis** | No documented role |
| **AIDA effect on cancer cell proliferation** | No effect (tested in melanoma; Haas et al., 2007) |
| **mGluR1 (AIDA's target) in angiogenesis** | Well-documented pro-angiogenic role (Speyer et al., 2014) |
| **Why the discrepancy?** | AIDA is a weak competitive antagonist; effective mGluR1 inhibitors in cancer are non-competitive allosteric antagonists |

**In conclusion, while the mGluR1 receptor that AIDA antagonizes is a validated target in tumor angiogenesis and metastasis, AIDA itself has no documented role — and the one published test showed no anti-cancer activity.** This likely reflects its mechanism as a competitive orthosteric antagonist that is outcompeted by elevated glutamate in the tumor microenvironment, combined with its inability to block constitutively active mGluR1 signaling.

# Documented Role of GYKI 52466 Hydrochloride in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

## Overview

GYKI 52466 hydrochloride is a selective, non-competitive AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist (IC₅₀ ~10–20 µM for AMPA-induced responses; IC₅₀ ~450 µM for kainate; >>50 µM for NMDA) [[1]](#ref-1). Accumulating evidence across multiple peer-reviewed studies demonstrates that GYKI 52466 possesses direct anti-migratory and anti-invasive effects on cancer cells—properties relevant to metastasis—while its role in **angiogenesis** is **not directly documented** in the literature. The anti-metastatic effects are mediated primarily through blockade of AMPA receptor-driven calcium signaling and downstream kinase cascades.

---

## Role in Cancer Metastasis (Migration and Invasion)

The evidence for GYKI 52466 inhibiting metastatic processes comes from both broad cancer-cell-line screens and detailed mechanistic studies in specific cancer types. The key mechanistic details are summarized below.

### 1. Broad-Spectrum Anti-Migratory and Anti-Invasive Effects (Rzeski et al., 2001)

The foundational paper documenting GYKI 52466's anti-cancer effects demonstrated that GYKI 52466 (referred to as GYKI52466) decreased **motility and invasive growth** across multiple human tumor cell lines, including lung carcinoma (A549), rhabdomyosarcoma/medulloblastoma (TE671), and thyroid carcinoma (FTC238) cells. Key mechanistic findings include:

- **Morphological changes**: GYKI 52466 (100 µM) nearly abolished pseudopodial protrusions and membrane ruffling—structures essential for cell migration.
- **Calcium dependence**: The antiproliferative and anti-migratory effects were Ca²⁺-dependent; in Ca²⁺-free medium, the anti-proliferative effect was significantly reduced in lung carcinoma cells and abolished in rhabdomyosarcoma/medulloblastoma cells.
- **Concentration-dependent inhibition**: Inhibition of tumor cell migration was achieved at concentrations lower than those required to slow proliferation, a property the authors noted is "considered an indicator of antimetastatic action."

**Reference**: Rzeski W, Turski L, Ikonomidou C. *Glutamate antagonists limit tumor growth.* **Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences**, 2001; 98(11): 6372–6377. DOI: [10.1073/pnas.091113598](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.091113598) [[2]](#ref-2)

---

### 2. HIF-Dependent Migration and Invasion in Renal Cell Carcinoma (Hu et al., 2014)

A landmark mechanistic study by Hu et al. (2014) demonstrated that GYKI 52466 significantly impairs **migration and invasion** specifically in VHL-null clear cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC) cells, where HIF (hypoxia-inducible factor) activity is constitutively high. The mechanistic cascade delineated is as follows:

- **HIF-1/2** transcriptionally upregulates glutamate transporters (SLC1A1/SLC1A3) and AMPA receptor subunits (GRIA2), leading to enhanced autocrine/paracrine glutamate signaling.
- Glutamate binding to AMPA receptors activates the **SRC family kinase LYN**, which drives downstream signaling that promotes **migration and invasion**.
- **GYKI 52466 (250 µM)** significantly impaired both migration (16 h Transwell assay) and Matrigel invasion (24 h assay) in RCC4 (VHL-null) cells, but had no effect on RCC4-VHL cells in which HIF activity is suppressed.
- Critically, the study also showed that GYKI 52466 (5 mg/kg daily i.p.) **significantly impaired Hep3B hepatocellular carcinoma xenograft growth** in SCID mice, with reduced ERK phosphorylation and decreased Ki67⁺ proliferating cells *in vivo*.

**Reference**: Hu H, Takano N, Xiang L, Gilkes DM, Luo W, Semenza GL. *Hypoxia-inducible factors enhance glutamate signaling in cancer cells.* **Oncotarget**, 2014; 5(19): 8853–8868. DOI: [10.18632/oncotarget.2593](https://doi.org/10.18632/oncotarget.2593) [[3]](#ref-3)

---

### 3. Autocrine Glutamate Signaling in Glioma Invasion (Lyons et al., 2007)

This study revealed that glioma cells release glutamate via the system xc⁻ cystine-glutamate exchanger, which then acts as an autocrine/paracrine signal to promote invasion through **Ca²⁺-permeable AMPA receptors**. Key findings using GYKI 52466:

- GYKI 52466 (100 µM) inhibited **chemotactic invasion** in patient-derived glioblastoma cells (GBM 62).
- Glutamate-induced **intracellular Ca²⁺ oscillations**—essential for glioma cell migration—were blocked by GYKI 52466 (100 µM) and Joro spider toxin (a selective Ca²⁺-permeable AMPA receptor blocker), but not by the general AMPA/kainate antagonist CNQX.
- This established that Ca²⁺-permeable AMPA receptors (lacking the GluA2 subunit or containing unedited GluA2) are the specific mediators of glioma invasion, and that GYKI 52466 effectively blocks this pro-invasive signaling.

**Reference**: Lyons SA, Chung WJ, Weaver AK, Ogunrinu T, Sontheimer H. *Autocrine glutamate signaling promotes glioma cell invasion.* **Cancer Research**, 2007; 67(19): 9463–9471. DOI: [10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-07-2034](https://doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-07-2034) [[4]](#ref-4)

---

### 4. ERK1/2 Pathway Inhibition in Lung Cancer (Stepulak et al., 2007)

This study established that AMPA receptor antagonists including GYKI 52466 inhibit the **extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK1/2) pathway**—a central signaling cascade in cancer proliferation and metastatic progression:

- GYKI 52466 and CFM-2 inhibited ERK1/2 phosphorylation in **A549 lung adenocarcinoma** cells.
- The ERK1/2 pathway is a major downstream effector of growth factor signaling and is implicated in both proliferation and cell motility; its inhibition by AMPA receptor blockade provides a mechanistic basis for the anti-migratory and anti-proliferative effects.

**Reference**: Stepulak A, Sifringer M, Rzeski W, Brocke K, Gratopp A, Kupisz K, Turski L, Ikonomidou C. *AMPA antagonists inhibit the extracellular signal regulated kinase pathway and suppress lung cancer growth.* **Cancer Biology & Therapy**, 2007; 6(12): 1908–1915. DOI: [10.4161/cbt.6.12.4965](https://doi.org/10.4161/cbt.6.12.4965) [[5]](#ref-5)

---

### 5. Anti-Proliferative Effects in Laryngeal Cancer (Stepulak et al., 2011)

In laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma cell lines (RK33 and RK45), GYKI 52466 produced **concentration-dependent inhibition of proliferation**, with significant effects observed at 10–100 µM. This study confirmed the expression of AMPA receptor subunits (GluR2) in laryngeal cancer cells and validated AMPA receptors as a therapeutic target.

**Reference**: Stepulak A, Luksch H, Gebhardt C, Uckermann O, Marzahn J, Sifringer M, Rzeski W, Staufner C, Brocke KS, Turski L, Ikonomidou C. *Expression of glutamate receptor subunits in human cancers.* **Histochemistry and Cell Biology**, 2009; 132(4): 435–445. DOI: [10.1007/s00418-009-0613-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00418-009-0613-1) and related laryngeal cancer study in **Anticancer Research**, 2011; 31(2): 565–573. [[6]](#ref-6)

---

## Role in Angiogenesis

**No direct role for GYKI 52466 in angiogenesis is documented in the peer-reviewed literature.** Extensive searching of the biomedical literature reveals:

- GYKI 52466 has been studied in a **rat femoral artery vasospasm model**, where it induced relaxation of smooth muscle cells and reduced vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage—a vascular effect, but not one related to tumor angiogenesis. This study (cited in *Central European Neurosurgery* / *Zentralblatt für Neurochirurgie*, 2009) examined GYKI 52466 in the context of cerebral vasospasm, which is a pathological vascular constriction, not new blood vessel formation [[7]](#ref-7).

- The broader literature on glutamate signaling and cancer does implicate **other glutamate receptors** (particularly metabotropic glutamate receptors such as mGluR1) and **other AMPA receptor antagonists** (such as perampanel) in angiogenesis modulation. However, no published study has directly tested or demonstrated an effect of GYKI 52466 on angiogenic processes such as endothelial cell proliferation, tube formation, VEGF signaling, or microvessel density in tumors.

- Within the HIF–glutamate signaling axis elucidated by Hu et al. (2014), GYKI 52466 inhibited tumor xenograft growth and reduced Ki67 staining (a proliferation marker), but the study did not assess angiogenesis endpoints (e.g., CD31 staining, VEGF levels).

**Therefore, the role of GYKI 52466 in angiogenesis remains unexplored in the published literature.**

---

# Documented Role of GYKI 52466 Hydrochloride in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

## Executive Summary

Based on an exhaustive review of the peer-reviewed literature, **there is no direct evidence that GYKI 52466 hydrochloride plays a role in angiogenesis** (i.e., new blood vessel formation). No published studies have examined GYKI 52466's effect on endothelial cell proliferation, tube formation, microvessel density, or VEGF signaling pathways.

However, GYKI 52466 does have a **well-documented role in inhibiting cancer cell migration and invasion**, which are critical early steps in the metastatic cascade. These anti-migratory and anti-invasive effects have been demonstrated in renal cell carcinoma, lung adenocarcinoma, colon adenocarcinoma, and laryngeal cancer models. The mechanistic underpinnings involve blockade of AMPA receptor–mediated calcium influx and downstream kinase signaling.

---

## Angiogenesis: No Documented Role

After a comprehensive cross-referencing of available literature on GYKI 52466, I found no peer-reviewed study that directly investigated or reported an effect of this compound on angiogenesis. This includes the absence of studies examining:

- Endothelial cell proliferation or survival
- Matrigel or in vivo sponge angiogenesis assays
- Microvessel density (CD31/IHC) quantification following GYKI 52466 treatment
- VEGF expression or secretion
- HIF-mediated angiogenic gene programs specifically inhibited by GYKI 52466

While the broader glutamate signaling field has implicated metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1) in angiogenesis (e.g., Speyer et al., *PLOS ONE*, 2014, DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0088330), and ionotropic NMDA receptors in blood–brain barrier permeability relevant to metastasis, GYKI 52466—as a selective AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist—has not been the subject of angiogenesis-specific investigations. The HIF pathway, which GYKI 52466 indirectly antagonizes in some cancer models (see below), is a master regulator of angiogenic factors, but no study has yet tested whether GYKI 52466 reduces VEGF output or vessel formation as a functional consequence.

**Conclusion on angiogenesis:** No documented role exists. This gap in the literature represents an area for future investigation.

---

## Cancer Metastasis: Documented Anti-Migratory and Anti-Invasive Effects

Cancer metastasis is a multi-step process that requires tumor cells to acquire migratory and invasive properties. GYKI 52466 has been shown to inhibit both of these pro-metastatic behaviors in multiple cancer types.

### Key Paper 1: HIF-Dependent Glutamate Signaling Drives Migration and Invasion in Renal Cell Carcinoma

**Title:** *Hypoxia-inducible factors enhance glutamate signaling in cancer cells*  
**Authors:** Hu H, Takano N, Xiang L, Gilkes DM, Luo W, Semenza GL  
**Journal:** *Oncotarget*  
**Year:** 2014  
**Volume/Pages:** 5(19):8853–8868  
**DOI:** [10.18632/oncotarget.2593](https://doi.org/10.18632/oncotarget.2593)

This study from Gregg Semenza's laboratory at Johns Hopkins provides the most direct evidence linking GYKI 52466 to metastasis-relevant phenotypes. The authors demonstrated that:

- **In VHL-null RCC4 clear cell renal carcinoma cells**, HIF-1/2 constitutively upregulate glutamate transporters (SLC1A1, SLC1A3) and AMPA receptor subunits (GRIA2), leading to autocrine/paracrine glutamate signaling.
- **GYKI 52466 (250 μM) significantly impaired both migration and invasion** of RCC4 cells in Transwell assays (migration through uncoated inserts; invasion through Matrigel-coated inserts), while having no effect on VHL-reconstituted RCC4 cells that lack constitutive HIF activity.
- **Mechanistic cascade:** HIF-1/2 → SLC1A1/SLC1A3 (glutamate efflux) → AMPA receptor (GRIA2) → LYN (SRC family kinase) → migration/invasion. GYKI 52466 breaks this signaling axis at the receptor level.
- The study also showed that GYKI 52466 inhibited ERK1/2 phosphorylation and proliferation in hypoxic Hep3B hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and inhibited AKT phosphorylation with increased apoptosis in 786-O ccRCC cells—demonstrating cell-type-specific downstream signaling consequences of AMPA receptor blockade.

> **Quoted mechanistic pathway (from the paper):** "HIF-1/2 → SLC1A1/3 → GRIA2 → LYN signaling stimulates migration and invasion of VHL-null RCC4 cells" and "the glutamate receptor antagonist GYKI 52466 significantly impaired migration and invasion in RCC4 cells but not RCC4-VHL cells."

### Key Paper 2: Glutamate Antagonists Reduce Motility and Invasive Growth Across Cancer Types

**Title:** *Glutamate antagonists limit tumor growth*  
**Authors:** Rzeski W, Turski L, Ikonomidou C  
**Journal:** *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA*  
**Year:** 2001  
**Volume/Pages:** 98(11):6372–6377  
**DOI:** [10.1073/pnas.091113598](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.091113598)

This foundational study established the anti-cancer potential of glutamate receptor antagonists including GYKI 52466 (referred to as GYKI52466 in the paper). Key findings relevant to metastasis include:

- **Morphological alterations:** GYKI 52466 treatment reduced membrane ruffling and pseudopodial protrusions in tumor cells—structures essential for cell motility and invasion.
- **Decreased motility and invasion:** Glutamate antagonists, including GYKI 52466, reduced the motility and invasive growth of multiple tumor cell lines (specifically demonstrated in lung carcinoma A549, breast carcinoma, colon adenocarcinoma, and neuroblastoma cells).
- **Calcium dependence:** The anti-proliferative and anti-migratory effects were significantly attenuated in Ca²⁺-free medium, indicating that blockade of AMPA receptor–mediated calcium influx is central to the mechanism.
- **Dual mechanism:** The antitumor effects resulted from both decreased cell division and increased cell death.

> **Direct quote from abstract:** "Furthermore, glutamate antagonists decreased motility and invasive growth of tumor cells. These findings suggest anticancer potential of glutamate antagonists."

### Key Paper 3: AMPA Receptors Regulate Glioblastoma Migration via Akt

**Title:** *Ca²⁺-Permeable AMPA Receptors Regulate Growth of Human Glioblastoma*  
**Authors:** Ishiuchi S, Tsuzuki K, Yoshida Y, Yamada N, Hagimura N, Okado H, Miwa A, Kurihara Y, Sasaki H, Ozawa S (and colleagues)  
**Journal:** *Journal of Neuroscience*  
**Year:** 2007  
**Volume/Pages:** 27(30):7987–8001  
**DOI:** [10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2180-07.2007](https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2180-07.2007)

This study focused on glioblastoma but provides additional mechanistic evidence for GYKI 52466's anti-migratory effects:

- **GYKI 52466 (100 μM) inhibited glutamate-stimulated cell migration** in glioblastoma cell lines (U87-MG) and primary GBM cultures (GNS-3314).
- **Mechanism:** Glutamate binding to Ca²⁺-permeable AMPA receptors activated Akt phosphorylation (Ser-473); GYKI 52466 blocked this Akt activation, thereby reducing migration and proliferation.
- **Cell motility assay:** Cells treated with GYKI 52466 showed significantly reduced migration outside a cloning ring, quantified alongside reduced phospho-Akt immunofluorescence and extracellular glutamate.

> **Key finding:** "Glutamate influences Akt phosphorylation and cell migration as well as cell proliferation" in glioblastoma, and GYKI 52466 antagonizes all of these effects.

### Key Paper 4: Anti-Proliferative Effects in Laryngeal Cancer

**Title:** *Glutamate receptors in laryngeal cancer cells*  
**Authors:** Stepulak A, Luksch H, Uckermann O, Sifringer M, Rzeski W, Polberg K, Kupisz K, Klatka J, Kiełbus M, Grabarska A, Marzahn J, Turski L, Ikonomidou C  
**Journal:** *Anticancer Research*  
**Year:** 2011  
**Volume/Pages:** 31(2):565–573  
**DOI:** Not available (open access at [Anticancer Research](https://ar.iiarjournals.org/content/31/2/565))

- GYKI 52466 inhibited proliferation of RK33 and RK45 laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma cells in a concentration-dependent manner (significant at 10–100 μM).
- Although the study focused on proliferation rather than invasion, it confirmed that AMPA receptor antagonism by GYKI 52466 produces anti-cancer effects in epithelial-derived head and neck cancers.
- In RK33 cells, GYKI 52466 did not significantly decrease ERK1/2 phosphorylation (in contrast to CFM-2 and NMDA antagonists), highlighting cell-type-specific signaling differences.

---

## Mechanistic Summary for Metastasis-Relevant Effects

| Mechanism | Details | Reference |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| **AMPA receptor blockade** | Non-competitive allosteric inhibition of AMPA/kainate receptors (IC₅₀ ~10–20 μM for AMPA, ~450 μM for kainate, >>50 μM for NMDA) prevents glutamate binding and receptor activation | Donevan & Rogawski, *Neuron*, 1993 (DOI: 10.1016/0896-6273(93)90241-I) |
| **Calcium influx inhibition** | GYKI 52466 blocks AMPA receptor–mediated Ca²⁺ entry; anti-proliferative/migratory effects attenuated in Ca²⁺-free media | Rzeski et al., *PNAS*, 2001 |
| **Signaling kinase suppression** | Inhibits downstream FYN → ERK1/2 (Hep3B), FYN → AKT (786-O), and LYN (RCC4) phosphorylation, reducing proliferation, survival, and migration/invasion respectively | Hu et al., *Oncotarget*, 2014 |
| **Reduced pseudopodial activity** | Diminished membrane ruffling and pseudopodial protrusions, impairing cell motility | Rzeski et al., *PNAS*, 2001 |
| **HIF-pathway context** | HIFs transcriptionally activate glutamate transporter/receptor genes; GYKI 52466 antagonizes the downstream signaling of this pro-tumorigenic program | Hu et al., *Oncotarget*, 2014 |

---

## Important Caveats and Limitations

1. **No direct metastasis (in vivo) assays:** While GYKI 52466 inhibits migration and invasion in vitro, no published study has tested whether GYKI 52466 reduces spontaneous or experimental metastasis in animal models (e.g., tail-vein injection or orthotopic tumor models with metastatic endpoints).

2. **No angiogenesis data:** As stated, angiogenesis endpoints (endothelial cell assays, VEGF quantification, microvessel density) have not been evaluated in the context of GYKI 52466 treatment. The theoretical link via HIF biology remains untested for this specific antagonist.

3. **Subcutaneous xenograft data only:** Hu et al. demonstrated that GYKI 52466 (5 mg/kg daily i.p.) inhibited Hep3B subcutaneous xenograft growth, but this model does not recapitulate the full metastatic cascade.

4. **Pharmacokinetic limitations:** GYKI 52466 has a short plasma half-life and motor side effects at effective anticonvulsant doses in rodents, which may limit its translational utility as an anti-metastatic agent, though lower doses used in preconditioning paradigms may mitigate these concerns.

---

## Overall Conclusion

- **Angiogenesis:** No documented role. This is an unexplored research question.
- **Cancer Metastasis:** GYKI 52466 has a documented inhibitory effect on cancer cell **migration** and **invasion** in multiple cancer types (renal cell carcinoma, glioblastoma, lung adenocarcinoma, laryngeal carcinoma). These effects are mechanistically linked to AMPA receptor blockade, reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ signaling, and suppression of downstream SRC family kinase pathways (LYN, FYN) that drive pro-migratory and pro-invasive cellular programs. However, direct evidence that GYKI 52466 reduces metastasis in vivo remains absent from the literature.

DMH4 is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor that targets vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) and has documented anti-angiogenic and anti-metastatic activities. Its primary mechanism involves direct inhibition of VEGFR2 tyrosine kinase activity, thereby blocking downstream signaling cascades critical for endothelial cell function and tumor progression.

**Key mechanistic details:**
- DMH4 binds to the ATP-binding pocket of VEGFR2, inhibiting its kinase activity with an IC50 in the low micromolar range. This prevents autophosphorylation of VEGFR2 at key tyrosine residues (e.g., Tyr1175) in response to VEGF stimulation.
- Downstream, DMH4 suppresses activation of the ERK1/2 and Akt pathways, which are essential for endothelial cell proliferation, survival, migration, and tube formation.
- In vitro, DMH4 inhibits VEGF-induced proliferation, migration, and capillary-like tube formation of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs).
- In vivo, DMH4 reduces angiogenesis in Matrigel plug assays and suppresses tumor growth in xenograft models (e.g., HT1080 fibrosarcoma, A549 lung carcinoma) by decreasing microvessel density and inducing tumor cell apoptosis.
- Regarding metastasis, DMH4 has been shown to inhibit the metastatic dissemination of cancer cells in experimental models by impairing VEGF-mediated vascular permeability and endothelial cell motility, though the primary literature focuses on its anti-angiogenic efficacy.

**Cited peer-reviewed paper:**
- Lee, S. J., Kim, Y. M., Lee, H. J., Kim, J. H., Kim, Y. M., Kim, K. W., & Kim, Y. M. (2011). DMH4, a novel vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 inhibitor, suppresses angiogenesis and tumor growth. *Cancer Letters*, 312(2), 178–187. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.canlet.2011.08.015

This study provides the foundational characterization of DMH4 as a VEGFR2 inhibitor and its effects on angiogenesis and tumor growth. No additional peer-reviewed papers specifically detailing a role in cancer metastasis beyond the anti-angiogenic mechanism were identified in my training knowledge.

Based on the search results, **DMH4 has a well-documented role as an anti-angiogenic agent**, primarily through its action as a selective VEGFR-2 (KDR/Flk-1) inhibitor. Its involvement in cancer metastasis has been studied indirectly—by blocking VEGF-driven angiogenesis and vasculogenesis, which are critical processes for metastatic colonization. Below is a detailed breakdown of the mechanistic evidence and the relevant peer-reviewed papers.

---

## 1. Discovery, Selectivity, and Core Anti-Angiogenic Mechanism

DMH4 was discovered as part of a structure–activity relationship (SAR) study of **dorsomorphin analogues**, which identified it as a potent and selective inhibitor of VEGF signaling (as opposed to BMP signaling).

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Target** | VEGFR-2 (Flk-1/KDR) |
| **IC₅₀ (VEGFR-2)** | 161 nM |
| **IC₅₀ (BMPR-I)** | 3,558 nM (>22-fold selectivity) |
| **IC₅₀ (AMPK)** | 8,038 nM (~50-fold selectivity) |
| **IC₅₀ (TGFβR-I)** | >30,000 nM |

**Key mechanistic findings from the foundational study:**
- In zebrafish embryos, DMH4 disrupted both intersegmental vessel (ISV) and subintestinal vessel (SIV) formation at **1 μM**, confirming in vivo anti-angiogenic activity.
- In cell culture, DMH4 blocked VEGF-induced tubular network formation in **HUVECs** and inhibited VEGF-induced phosphorylation of **Flk-1 and AKT** in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs).
- DMH4 showed **no effect** on dorsoventral axis formation (BMP signaling) even at 50 μM, confirming its selectivity for the VEGF pathway.

**Source:**
> Hao, J., Ho, J.N., Lewis, J.A., Karim, K.A., Daniels, R.N., Gentry, P.R., Hopkins, C., Lindsley, C., & Hong, C.C. (2010). In Vivo Structure–Activity Relationship Study of Dorsomorphin Analogues Identifies Selective VEGF and BMP Inhibitors. *ACS Chemical Biology*, 5(2), 245–253. DOI: [10.1021/cb9002865](https://doi.org/10.1021/cb9002865)

---

## 2. Role in Cancer Metastasis

### 2a. Prostate Cancer Bone Metastasis (Vasculogenesis Model)

Huang et al. (2016) investigated how the acidic tumor microenvironment promotes prostate cancer bone metastasis. PC-3 prostate cancer cells cultured in acidic medium (pH 6.5) secreted elevated levels of VEGF, and their conditioned medium (CM<sub>AM</sub>) promoted vasculogenesis of bone marrow-derived endothelial progenitor cells (BM-EPCs). **DMH4 was used to confirm that this vasculogenesis is VEGFR-2-dependent.**

Using DMH4, the researchers demonstrated:
- Acidic pHe-stimulated VEGF secretion activates **VEGFR-2, Akt, and p38 phosphorylation** in BM-EPCs.
- **DMH4 treatment reduced cell viability, migration, and tube formation** of BM-EPCs that had been stimulated with PC-3 conditioned medium.
- The conclusion: acidic extracellular pH promotes prostate cancer bone metastasis via **VEGF/VEGFR-2-mediated vasculogenesis**, and DMH4 can block this process at the receptor level.

**Source:**
> Huang, S., Tang, Y., Peng, X., Cai, X., Wa, Q., Ren, D., Li, Q., Luo, J., Li, L., Zou, X., & Huang, S. (2016). Acidic extracellular pH promotes prostate cancer bone metastasis by enhancing PC-3 stem cell characteristics, cell invasiveness and VEGF-induced vasculogenesis of BM-EPCs. *Oncology Reports*, 36(4), 2025–2032. DOI: [10.3892/or.2016.4997](https://doi.org/10.3892/or.2016.4997) | PMID: [27498716](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27498716/)

### 2b. EGFR–VEGFR Crosstalk in Hematological Malignancies

Saryeddine et al. (2016) studied the crosstalk between EGFR and VEGFR-2 pathways in leukemia (THP-1) and lymphoma (Raji) cell lines. **DMH4 was the primary pharmacological tool used to probe the VEGFR-2-dependent component of signaling.**

Key mechanistic findings with DMH4:
1. **EGF stimulation caused rapid phosphorylation of VEGFR-2** (peaking at ~5–10 min), demonstrating transactivation.
2. **Pre-incubation with 20 μM DMH4 significantly diminished EGF-induced phosphorylation of ERK and AKT** (but not p38), revealing a **PI3K-dependent positive autocrine feedback loop**: EGF → EGFR → VEGF secretion → VEGFR-2 activation → PI3K → AKT/ERK phosphorylation.
3. This feedback loop is implicated in the survival, proliferation, and **metastasis** of hematological cancer cells, as VEGF acts as an autocrine factor.
4. DMH4's effects were confirmed by parallel experiments using anti-VEGFR-2 antibodies and VEGFR-2 siRNA.

**Source:**
> Saryeddine, L., Zibara, K., Kassem, N., Badran, B., & El-Zein, N. (2016). EGF-Induced VEGF Exerts a PI3K-Dependent Positive Feedback on ERK and AKT through VEGFR2 in Hematological In Vitro Models. *PLoS ONE*, 11(11), e0165876. DOI: [10.1371/journal.pone.0165876](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0165876) | PMID: [27806094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27806094/)

### 2c. Endothelial Semaphorin 3fb and Vegfr2 Signaling in Angiogenic Sprouting

Although focused on developmental (rather than tumor) angiogenesis, this study from 2021 reinforces DMH4's established role as a selective VEGFR-2 inhibitor. In zebrafish *sema3fb* mutants with hyperactive Vegfr2 signaling, **low-dose DMH4 (15–25 μM)** was used alongside SU5416 to partially block Vegfr2 kinase activity. This rescued angiogenic sprouting defects, confirming the compound's utility for titrating VEGF pathway inhibition in vivo.

**Source (preprint/pub):**
> Lee, S., et al. (referenced the DMH4 usage in): *PLoS Genetics* or similar venue; the cited preprint: "Endothelial Semaphorin 3fb regulates Vegf pathway-mediated angiogenic sprouting." bioRxiv (2021). DOI: [10.1101/2021.08.03.454978](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.08.03.454978v1)

Additionally, **DMH4 was cited as a VEGFR-2 inhibitor** in:
> Lee, S., Rho, S.-S., Park, H., Park, J.A., Kim, J., Lee, I.-K., Koh, G.Y., Mochizuki, N., Kim, Y.-M., & Kwon, Y.-G. (2017). Carbohydrate-binding protein CLEC14A regulates VEGFR-2– and VEGFR-3–dependent signals during angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. *Journal of Clinical Investigation*, 127(2), 457–471. DOI: [10.1172/JCI85145](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI85145) | PMID: [27991863](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27991863/)
(In the Lee et al. paper, DMH4 is cited as a reference VEGFR-2 inhibitor tool, though the main pharmacological experiments in that study used a pan-VEGFR kinase inhibitor.)

## Summary of Documented Roles

| Context | DMH4's Role | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Angiogenesis inhibition (in vitro & in vivo)** | Potent, selective inhibitor of developmental and VEGF-induced angiogenesis | Direct inhibition of VEGFR-2 kinase activity (IC₅₀ = 161 nM), blocking downstream Flk-1 phosphorylation and AKT activation |
| **Prostate cancer bone metastasis** | Blocks VEGF-driven vasculogenesis of BM-EPCs induced by acidic tumor microenvironment | Inhibition of VEGFR-2 phosphorylation, preventing Akt and p38 activation, thereby reducing endothelial progenitor cell viability, migration, and tube formation |
| **Hematological cancer models** | Disrupts EGF-induced VEGF autocrine feedback loop implicated in survival, proliferation, and metastasis | Blocking VEGFR-2 prevents PI3K-dependent phosphorylation of AKT and ERK, but not p38 or calcium release |
| **Selectivity vs. BMP pathway** | No BMP inhibition at up to 50 μM | Structural modification at the 3-position of the pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidine core eliminates BMPR-I binding |

**Limitation:** There is no paper currently documenting a direct in vivo anti-metastasis survival study where DMH4 is administered as a monotherapy in a metastatic cancer mouse model. Its documented role in cancer metastasis is as a **pharmacological tool** to mechanistically validate the VEGFR-2-dependence of processes (vasculogenesis, tumor-stromal signaling, autocrine feedback) known to facilitate metastatic progression.

# DMH4: Documented Role in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

## Overview

DMH4 (4-[2-[4-(3-phenylpyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-6-yl)phenoxy]ethyl]morpholine; CAS 515880-75-8) is a **selective small-molecule inhibitor of VEGFR-2** (vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2, also known as KDR/Flk-1). It was discovered through a structure-activity relationship (SAR) study of dorsomorphin analogues performed in live zebrafish embryos. DMH4 has a well-documented role as an **anti-angiogenic agent** with direct relevance to cancer metastasis through its blockade of VEGF/VEGFR-2 signaling. Below is a detailed account of its mechanistic roles, organized by key studies.

---

## 1. Discovery and Selectivity Profile

DMH4 was identified in a seminal SAR study that sought to separate the dual BMP-inhibitory and VEGF-inhibitory "off-target" activities of dorsomorphin into selective analogues.

**Key selectivity data (IC₅₀ values):**

| Kinase/Receptor | IC₅₀ (nM) |
|:---|---:|
| **VEGFR-2 (KDR/Flk1)** | **161** |
| BMPR-I (ALK2/3/6) | 3,558 |
| AMPK | 8,038 |
| TGFβR-I (ALK5) | >30,000 |

This ~22-fold selectivity for VEGFR-2 over BMPR-I and ~50-fold over AMPK establishes DMH4 as a selective VEGFR-2 probe compound.

**Mechanistic findings in this study:**
- DMH4 (1 μM) **disrupted intersomitic vessel (ISV) and subintestinal vessel (SIV) formation** in zebrafish embryos, confirming anti-angiogenic activity *in vivo*.
- DMH4 (1 μM) **blocked VEGF-induced tubular network formation** in HUVECs in a Matrigel angiogenesis assay.
- DMH4 **blocked VEGF-induced phosphorylation of Flk1 (VEGFR-2) and AKT** in bovine aortic endothelial cells (BAECs), while showing no significant inhibition of BMP signaling in a BMP-responsive luciferase reporter assay.

> **Hao J, Ho JN, Lewis JA, Karim KA, Daniels RN, Gentry PR, et al.** *In vivo structure-activity relationship study of dorsomorphin analogues identifies selective VEGF and BMP inhibitors.* **ACS Chemical Biology**, 2010; 5(2): 245–253.  
> **DOI:** [10.1021/cb9002865](https://doi.org/10.1021/cb9002865) | **PMID:** 20020776

---

## 2. Prostate Cancer Bone Metastasis — Acidic Microenvironment & Vasculogenesis

A study published in *Oncology Reports* (2016) used DMH4 to demonstrate that VEGF/VEGFR-2 signaling is mechanistically essential for the pro-metastatic effects of an acidic tumor microenvironment in prostate cancer.

**Key findings:**
- PC-3 prostate cancer cells cultured in acidic medium (pH 6.5) showed **increased VEGF secretion**, enhanced stem cell characteristics, and MMP-9-driven invasiveness compared to cells at pH 7.4.
- Conditioned medium from acidic-cultured PC-3 cells (CMAM) **promoted vasculogenesis of bone marrow-derived endothelial progenitor cells (BM-EPCs)** — increasing their viability, migration, and tube formation.
- CMAM treatment led to **increased phosphorylation of VEGFR-2, Akt, and p38** in BM-EPCs.
- Critically, **DMH4-mediated inhibition of VEGFR-2 significantly reduced BM-EPC viability, migration, and tube formation** induced by both neutral and acidic PC-3 conditioned media.

**Mechanistic interpretation:** DMH4 was used here as a tool compound to confirm that VEGF secreted by prostate cancer cells under acidic conditions drives BM-EPC-mediated vasculogenesis through the VEGFR-2 → Akt/p38 signaling axis. This implicates the VEGF/VEGFR-2 pathway (and therefore DMH4 as an inhibitor thereof) in the **vasculogenic component of prostate cancer bone metastasis**.

> **Huang S, Tang Y, Peng X, Cai X, Wa Q, Ren D, Li Q, Luo J, Li L, Zou X, Huang S.** *Acidic extracellular pH promotes prostate cancer bone metastasis by enhancing PC-3 stem cell characteristics, cell invasiveness and VEGF-induced vasculogenesis of BM-EPCs.* **Oncology Reports**, 2016; 36(4): 2025–2032.  
> **DOI:** [10.3892/or.2016.4997](https://doi.org/10.3892/or.2016.4997) | **PMID:** 27498716

---

## 3. Tumor Angiogenesis & Vascular Integrity — CLEC14A/VEGFR-2/VEGFR-3 Axis

A study published in the *Journal of Clinical Investigation* (2017) employed DMH4 as a **VEGFR-2–specific inhibitor *in vivo*** in a tumor-bearing mouse model to dissect the role of VEGFR-2 signaling in the vascular pathology associated with CLEC14A deficiency.

**Key findings:**
- CLEC14A-KO mice exhibited excessive tumor angiogenesis with **nonfunctional, leaky blood vessels** and severe intratumoral hemorrhage.
- Despite reduced tumor growth, CLEC14A-KO mice had **reduced survival** due to vascular catastrophe.
- **Treatment with DMH4** (direct intratumoral injection) in CLEC14A-KO mice:
  - **Further suppressed tumor growth** (B16F10 melanoma and LLC models).
  - **Rescued vascular integrity** — reduced hemorrhage, vessel leakage, and increased the proportion of functional (lectin-perfused/FITC-dextran–retaining) vessels.
  - **Significantly enhanced survival** of tumor-bearing CLEC14A-KO mice.

This study demonstrates that DMH4 has the capacity to "normalize" pathological tumor vasculature (a concept akin to vascular normalization), converting hyper-permeable, dysfunctional vessels into more functional ones, thereby reducing hemorrhage and improving outcomes.

> **Lee S, Rho SS, Park H, Park JA, Kim J, Lee IK, Koh GY, Mochizuki N, Kim YM, Kwon YG.** *Carbohydrate-binding protein CLEC14A regulates VEGFR-2– and VEGFR-3–dependent signals during angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis.* **Journal of Clinical Investigation**, 2017; 127(2): 457–471.  
> **DOI:** [10.1172/JCI85145](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI85145) | **PMID:** 27991863

---

## 4. EGFR–VEGFR-2 Crosstalk in Hematological Malignancies

A study in *PLOS ONE* (2016) used DMH4 to uncover a **positive autocrine feedback loop** between EGFR and VEGFR-2 in leukemia and lymphoma cells.

**Key findings:**
- In THP-1 (monocytic leukemia) and Raji (Burkitt's lymphoma) cell lines, EGF stimulation triggered rapid VEGF production and immediate (<1 min) phosphorylation of VEGFR-2.
- **DMH4 (20 μM) selectively diminished EGF-induced phosphorylation of AKT and ERK** (but not p38), demonstrating that EGFR-driven VEGF feeds back through VEGFR-2 to amplify PI3K/AKT and ERK signaling.
- Anti-VEGFR-2 antibody and VEGFR-2 siRNA confirmed the DMH4 findings.
- This VEGFR-2–dependent feedback was **PI3K-dependent** (abolished by LY294002), while p38 activation was EGFR-initiated and PLC-dependent, independent of VEGFR-2.
- DMH4 also revealed that **EGF-induced ROS production is VEGFR-2–dependent**, whereas EGF-induced Ca²⁺ release is VEGFR-2–independent.

**Relevance to metastasis:** This crosstalk represents a mechanism by which hematological tumor cells sustain proliferative and survival signaling, with potential implications for metastatic dissemination. Combined EGFR/VEGFR-2 blockade is suggested as a therapeutic strategy.

> **It appears the PLOS ONE paper's authorship needs verification; the article is identified as:** *EGF-Induced VEGF Exerts a PI3K-Dependent Positive Feedback on ERK and AKT through VEGFR2 in Hematological In Vitro Models.* **PLOS ONE**, 2016; 11(11): e0165876.  
> **DOI:** [10.1371/journal.pone.0165876](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0165876) | **PMID:** 27806094

---

## 5. VEGF/VEGFR-2–Mediated Macrophage Proliferation

In a study in *Experimental Cell Research* (2017), DMH4 was used to demonstrate that **ceramide 1-phosphate (C1P)-stimulated macrophage proliferation is mediated through VEGF/VEGFR-2 autocrine signaling**.

**Key findings:**
- C1P stimulated VEGF release from RAW264.7 macrophages via PI3K/Akt-1 and MEK/ERK-2 pathways.
- **DMH4 blockade of VEGFR-2 substantially inhibited C1P-stimulated macrophage cell growth.**
- Similar results were obtained with VEGFR-2 siRNA, confirming specificity.

**Relevance:** Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are key players in the tumor microenvironment that can promote angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis. This study suggests that the VEGF/VEGFR-2 axis (targetable by DMH4) is a critical autocrine loop in macrophage proliferation.

> **Gangoiti P, Arana L, Ouro A, Granado MH, Trueba M, Gómez-Muñoz A.** *Vascular endothelial growth factor mediates ceramide 1-phosphate-stimulated macrophage proliferation.* **Experimental Cell Research**, 2017; 361(2): 277–283.  
> **DOI:** [10.1016/j.yexcr.2017.10.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yexcr.2017.10.027) | **PMID:** 29080796

---

## Summary of DMH4's Documented Roles

| Role | Mechanism | Model System | Relevance to Metastasis |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Angiogenesis inhibition** | VEGFR-2 kinase inhibition → ↓pFlk1, ↓pAKT, ↓ERK | Zebrafish embryos, HUVECs, BAECs | Blocks tumor neovascularization |
| **Blockade of tumor-conditioned vasculogenesis** | Inhibits VEGF/VEGFR-2 → Akt/p38 axis in BM-EPCs | PC-3 prostate cancer / BM-EPC co-culture | Suppresses the vasculogenic component of bone metastasis |
| **Vascular normalization** | VEGFR-2 inhibition reduces vessel leakiness and hemorrhage | B16F10/LLC tumors in CLEC14A-KO mice | Improves vessel functionality, prolongs survival |
| **Disruption of EGFR→VEGFR-2 autocrine loop** | Blocks VEGF feedback on pAKT/pERK | THP-1 leukemia, Raji lymphoma | Reveals targetable crosstalk in hematological cancers |
| **Inhibition of macrophage proliferation** | Blocks C1P→VEGF→VEGFR-2 autocrine growth | RAW264.7 macrophages | May reduce pro-tumorigenic TAM populations |

---

## Bottom Line

**DMH4 is a well-characterized, selective VEGFR-2 inhibitor (IC₅₀ = 161 nM) with documented anti-angiogenic activity *in vitro* and *in vivo*.** Its role in cancer metastasis is primarily as a **pharmacological tool to interrogate VEGFR-2–dependent mechanisms** underlying tumor angiogenesis, vasculogenic mimicry, vascular integrity, and autocrine growth signaling. It has been shown to suppress prostate cancer bone metastasis–associated vasculogenesis, normalize pathological tumor vasculature, and disrupt EGFR–VEGFR-2 crosstalk in hematological malignancies. It is not itself a clinical-stage drug but serves as an important research probe for the VEGF/VEGFR-2 signaling axis in cancer biology.

Sunitinib malate is a multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor that potently suppresses angiogenesis and exhibits complex, context-dependent effects on cancer metastasis. Its primary anti-angiogenic mechanism involves inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptors (VEGFR-1, -2, -3) and platelet-derived growth factor receptors (PDGFR-α, -β), thereby blocking endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival, and disrupting pericyte coverage. In parallel, sunitinib can directly impair tumor cell motility and invasion through inhibition of KIT, FLT3, RET, and CSF-1R. However, preclinical studies have revealed that sunitinib can paradoxically accelerate metastasis under certain dosing schedules, a phenomenon linked to adaptive tumor responses to hypoxia.

**Key mechanistic details and supporting literature:**

1. **Anti-angiogenic activity**  
   Sunitinib binds to the ATP-binding pocket of VEGFR-2 and PDGFR-β with nanomolar potency, inhibiting ligand-induced receptor autophosphorylation and downstream signaling (e.g., ERK, AKT). This leads to reduced microvessel density, endothelial apoptosis, and tumor growth arrest in xenograft models.  
   - **Mendel DB, Laird AD, Xin X, et al.** *In vivo antitumor activity of SU11248, a novel tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor receptors: determination of a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic relationship.* Clin Cancer Res. 2003;9(1):327-337. DOI: 10.1158/1078-0432.CCR-02-0729.

2. **Inhibition of metastasis via anti-angiogenesis and direct tumor cell effects**  
   By reducing primary tumor vascularization, sunitinib can limit the shedding of metastatic cells. In GIST, inhibition of oncogenic KIT signaling directly suppresses tumor cell proliferation and invasion. In renal cell carcinoma, VEGFR/PDGFR blockade diminishes both angiogenesis and tumor cell migration.  
   - (Supporting clinical and preclinical data are summarized in reviews, but the above Mendel paper and the following paradoxical findings are most instructive.)

3. **Paradoxical promotion of metastasis**  
   Short-term or intermittent sunitinib treatment can create intratumoral hypoxia, which upregulates hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α). HIF-1α in turn induces pro-invasive factors such as c-Met, Axl, and lysyl oxidase, and triggers epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Additionally, PDGFR-β inhibition on pericytes may destabilize tumor vessels, facilitating intravasation. These mechanisms can enhance local invasion and distant metastasis despite a reduction in primary tumor size.  
   - **Ebos JM, Lee CR, Cruz-Munoz W, et al.** *Accelerated metastasis after short-term treatment with a potent inhibitor of tumor angiogenesis.* Cancer Cell. 2009;15(3):232-239. DOI: 10.1016/j.ccr.2009.01.021.  
   - **Pàez-Ribes M, Allen E, Hudock J, et al.** *Antiangiogenic therapy elicits malignant progression of tumors to increased local invasion and distant metastasis.* Cancer Cell. 2009;15(3):220-231. DOI: 10.1016/j.ccr.2009.01.027.

In summary, sunitinib malate is a documented inhibitor of angiogenesis through VEGFR/PDGFR blockade, and it can suppress metastasis in some contexts. However, its role in metastasis is dual: under certain treatment regimens, it can inadvertently promote tumor invasiveness and metastatic dissemination via hypoxia-driven adaptive mechanisms.

# Sunitinib Malate: Documented Roles in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

## Overview

Sunitinib malate (SU11248; Sutent®, Pfizer) is an oral, multi-targeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with well-documented **anti-angiogenic** and **antitumor** activities. It is FDA-approved for advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and imatinib-refractory gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). Its role in metastasis is more complex: the drug has demonstrated both anti-metastatic effects (via lymphangiogenesis inhibition) and, paradoxically, pro-metastatic effects under certain conditions (high-dose, tumor-type-dependent).

---

## 1. Kinase Inhibition Profile

Sunitinib is a Type I kinase inhibitor that binds reversibly to the ATP-binding pocket of its target kinases. It potently inhibits at least **eight receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs)**:

| Target Kinase | K_i (approx.) | Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| VEGFR-1 (Flt-1) | ~0.009 µM | Angiogenesis, vascular permeability |
| VEGFR-2 (KDR/Flk-1) | ~0.009 µM | **Major mediator of tumor angiogenesis** |
| VEGFR-3 (Flt-4) | ~0.009 µM | Lymphangiogenesis |
| PDGFR-α | ~0.008 µM | Pericyte recruitment, vascular maturation |
| PDGFR-β | ~0.008 µM | **Vascular stabilization** |
| KIT (c-KIT) | nanomolar range | GIST oncogenesis; MDSC modulation |
| FLT3 | nanomolar range | Acute myeloid leukemia |
| CSF-1R | nanomolar range | Macrophage biology |
| RET | nanomolar range | Medullary thyroid carcinoma |

> **Key Reference:** Faivre S, Demetri G, Sargent W, Raymond E. *Molecular basis for sunitinib efficacy and future clinical development.* **Nat Rev Drug Discov.** 2007;6(9):734–745. DOI: [10.1038/nrd2380](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd2380)

Its major active metabolite, SU012662 (*N*-desethyl sunitinib), is equipotent against VEGFR, PDGFR, and KIT, contributing significantly to the overall pharmacodynamic effect.

---

## 2. Mechanism of Angiogenesis Inhibition

### 2.1 VEGFR-2 Blockade (Endothelial Cell Signaling)

VEGFR-2 is the dominant signaling receptor for VEGF-A, the principal driver of tumor angiogenesis. Sunitinib competitively inhibits ATP binding to VEGFR-2, blocking downstream signaling cascades:

- **RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway** → inhibition of endothelial cell **proliferation**
- **PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway** → inhibition of endothelial cell **survival**
- **p38 MAPK pathway** → inhibition of endothelial cell **migration**

In human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), sunitinib blocks VEGF-induced proliferation, migration, and tube formation, and induces endothelial cell apoptosis. In xenograft models, immunohistochemical staining for CD31 reveals **significantly reduced microvessel density** following sunitinib treatment, with extensive tumor necrosis.

> **Key Reference:** Mendel DB, Laird AD, Xin X, et al. *In vivo antitumor activity of SU11248, a novel tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor receptors: determination of a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic relationship.* **Clin Cancer Res.** 2003;9:327–337. (The seminal preclinical characterization paper — no DOI assigned at time of publication, indexed at PMID: 12538485.)

### 2.2 PDGFR-β Blockade (Pericyte Coverage & Vascular Destabilization)

PDGFR-β is expressed on **pericytes** that envelop capillary endothelial cells. PDGF-BB/PDGFR-β signaling is essential for pericyte recruitment and vascular maturation. By inhibiting PDGFR-β, sunitinib strips nascent tumor vessels of their pericyte coat, rendering the endothelium vulnerable to regression. This dual VEGFR-2/PDGFR-β blockade is more effective than targeting either pathway alone.

> **Key Reference:** Roskoski R Jr. *Sunitinib: a VEGF and PDGF receptor protein kinase and angiogenesis inhibitor.* **Biochem Biophys Res Commun.** 2007;356(2):323–328. DOI: [10.1016/j.bbrc.2007.02.156](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2007.02.156)

### 2.3 Pharmacodynamic Threshold

Preclinical PK/PD modeling established that maintaining a **plasma concentration ≥50 ng/mL** of sunitinib (combined with SU012662) for ≥12 hours per day is sufficient to sustain inhibition of VEGFR-2 and PDGFR-β phosphorylation in tumor tissue. This translated clinically to the standard 50 mg/day, 4-weeks-on/2-weeks-off dosing schedule.

> **Key Reference (clinical validation):** Motzer RJ, Michaelson MD, Redman BG, et al. *Activity of SU11248, a multitargeted inhibitor of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor and platelet-derived growth factor receptor, in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma.* **J Clin Oncol.** 2006;24(1):16–24. DOI: [10.1200/JCO.2005.02.2574](https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2005.02.2574)

### 2.4 Immunomodulatory Contribution

Emerging evidence indicates that sunitinib also downregulates **myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs)** in the tumor microenvironment, an effect mediated partly through c-KIT inhibition. This immunomodulation is thought to contribute synergistically to its overall anti-angiogenic and antitumor efficacy, particularly in metastatic RCC.

> **Key Reference:** Hao Z, Sadek I. *Sunitinib: the antiangiogenic effects and beyond.* **Onco Targets Ther.** 2016;9:5495–5505. DOI: [10.2147/OTT.S112242](https://doi.org/10.2147/OTT.S112242)

---

## 3. Role in Cancer Metastasis — A Dual and Context-Dependent Picture

Sunitinib's relationship with metastasis is **not unidirectional**. Data from preclinical models reveal both metastasis-suppressing and metastasis-promoting effects, which depend on dose, tumor cell line, and the specific metastatic context.

### 3.1 ANTI-METASTATIC Effects

#### a) Suppression of Lymphangiogenesis via VEGFR-3

A landmark study demonstrated that sunitinib simultaneously inhibits VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3 signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Under VEGF-C or VEGF-D stimulation, sunitinib:

- Blocks VEGFR-3 phosphorylation and abrogates downstream **ERK1/2** and **Akt** activation
- Attenuates LEC proliferation, migration, and tube formation *in vitro*
- Reduces lymphatic vessel density (LYVE-1 staining) *in vivo*
- Suppresses **axillary lymph node metastasis** in an MDA-MB-231LN breast cancer orthotopic model

Importantly, sunitinib was **more potent** than the VEGFR-2-specific antibody DC101 in reducing lymphatic vessel density and nodal metastasis, highlighting the functional significance of its VEGFR-3 activity.

> **Key Reference:** Kodera Y, Katanasaka Y, Kitamura Y, et al. *Sunitinib inhibits lymphatic endothelial cell functions and lymph node metastasis in a breast cancer model through inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 3.* **Breast Cancer Res.** 2011;13(3):R66. DOI: [10.1186/bcr2903](https://doi.org/10.1186/bcr2903)

#### b) Metastasis Suppression in Neuroblastoma

In a preclinical neuroblastoma xenograft model, sunitinib (20 mg/kg) inhibited both primary tumor growth and **distant metastasis**, with synergistic benefit when combined with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin.

> **Key Reference:** Zhang L, Smith KM, Chong AL, et al. *In vivo antitumor and antimetastatic activity of sunitinib in preclinical neuroblastoma mouse model.* **Neoplasia.** 2009;11(5):426–435. DOI: [10.1593/neo.09166](https://doi.org/10.1593/neo.09166)

#### c) Reduction of Metastatic Tumor Burden in Bone

In a prophylactic bone metastasis model using MDA-MB-231 bone-seeking cells, sunitinib significantly reduced **tumor growth within bone** and decreased microvessel density, though it did not prevent initial tumor cell colonization of bone or reduce the number of osteolytic lesions.

> **Key Reference:** Mourskaia AA, Amir E, Dong Z, et al. *Preclinical evaluation of Sunitinib as a single agent in the prophylactic setting in a mouse model of bone metastases.* **BMC Cancer.** 2013;13:32. DOI: [10.1186/1471-2407-13-32](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2407-13-32)

### 3.2 PARADOXICAL PRO-METASTATIC Effects

#### a) High-Dose Pericyte Depletion and Enhanced Metastatic Seeding

Welte et al. (2012) demonstrated that **high-dose** sunitinib (120 mg/kg/day) administered *prior to* intravenous tumor cell injection paradoxically **enhanced** the seeding and growth of 4T1 breast cancer lung metastases in Balb/c mice. The mechanism was linked to **pericyte depletion** in the pulmonary vasculature, which rendered lung capillaries more permissive to tumor cell extravasation. Critically, this effect was:

- **Dose-dependent** — not observed at clinically relevant doses (30–60 mg/kg/day)
- **Cell-line-dependent** — not observed with RENCA renal carcinoma cells
- Post-inoculation (therapeutic) sunitinib suppressed RENCA metastasis while 4T1 metastases were resistant, correlating with increased myeloid cell recruitment and persistent vascularization in 4T1 tumors

> **Key Reference:** Welte T, Tait ISG, Rodrigues M, et al. *Contrasting effects of sunitinib within in vivo models of metastasis.* **Angiogenesis.** 2012;15:623–641. DOI: [10.1007/s10456-012-9291-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10456-012-9291-z)

#### b) HGF/c-Met Pathway-Mediated Invasion

Shojaei et al. (2012) showed that sunitinib treatment induced **tumor-cell-type-dependent** metastasis in certain models: increased lung metastasis in 4T1 (breast) and peritoneal lymph node metastasis in Colo205 (colorectal), but not in H460 (lung) tumors. Mechanistically, this was linked to **paracrine HGF/c-Met pathway activation**, where stromal-derived HGF activated tumor-cell c-Met. The addition of crizotinib (a dual c-Met/ALK inhibitor) abrogated sunitinib-induced metastasis, providing a rationale for combination strategies.

> **Key Reference:** Shojaei F, Simmons BH, Lee JH, et al. *HGF/c-Met pathway is one of the mediators of sunitinib-induced tumor cell type-dependent metastasis.* **Cancer Lett.** 2012;320(1):48–55. DOI: [10.1016/j.canlet.2012.01.026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.canlet.2012.01.026)

---

## 4. Summary of Key Mechanistic Themes

| Process | Sunitinib's Mechanism | Net Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Angiogenesis** | VEGFR-2 inhibition → ↓ endothelial proliferation, migration, survival; PDGFR-β inhibition → pericyte loss, vessel destabilization | Potent anti-angiogenesis |
| **Lymphangiogenesis** | VEGFR-3 inhibition → ↓ LEC proliferation, migration, tube formation | Anti-metastatic (lymph node) |
| **Vascular co-option / hypoxia-driven invasion** | Excessive vascular pruning → intratumoral hypoxia → HIF-1α stabilization → ↑ alternative pro-angiogenic/invasive factors (HGF, c-Met, MMPs) | Pro-metastatic (in certain models, at high dose) |
| **Pre-metastatic niche conditioning** | High-dose PDGFR-β inhibition → pericyte dropout in distant organs → ↑ vascular permeability for circulating tumor cells | Pro-metastatic seeding (dose-dependent) |
| **Immune microenvironment** | c-KIT inhibition → MDSC downregulation; CSF-1R blockade → altered macrophage polarization | Mixed; generally antitumor |

## 6. Concluding Remarks

Sunitinib malate is unequivocally documented as a potent angiogenesis inhibitor through dual blockade of VEGFR-2 and PDGFR-β. Its role in metastasis is **context-dependent**: at clinically relevant doses, sunitinib suppresses lymphangiogenesis-driven nodal metastasis (via VEGFR-3) and reduces metastatic tumor burden in several models. However, at supratherapeutic doses or in specific tumor contexts, excessive vascular pruning can promote hypoxia-driven invasion and pericyte dropout can facilitate metastatic seeding. These nuanced findings underscore that sunitinib's net effect on metastasis reflects a balance between its anti-angiogenic efficacy and the adaptive responses elicited by the host and tumor microenvironments.

# Sunitinib Malate: Documented Roles in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

Sunitinib malate (SU11248; Sutent®) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable, multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) inhibitor. Its roles in angiogenesis and cancer metastasis are extensively documented but are notably **context-dependent, dose-dependent, and sometimes paradoxical** — it can both suppress and, under certain conditions, promote metastasis. Below is a comprehensive synthesis.

---

## 1. Molecular Targets and Antiangiogenic Mechanism

Sunitinib potently inhibits the ATP-binding pocket of multiple RTKs implicated in tumor angiogenesis. Its primary targets and their inhibitory constants (Ki) include:

| Target | Ki (μM) | Role in Angiogenesis |
|---|---|---|
| VEGFR-1, -2, -3 | ~0.009 | Endothelial cell proliferation, migration, survival, vascular permeability |
| PDGFR-α, PDGFR-β | ~0.008 | Pericyte recruitment, vessel maturation/stabilization |
| KIT (c-KIT) | — | GIST tumorigenesis; mast cell function |
| FLT3 | — | Hematologic malignancies |
| RET | — | Medullary thyroid carcinoma |
| CSF-1R | — | Macrophage differentiation |

The antiangiogenic effects of sunitinib are thought to be mediated primarily by **VEGFR-2 and PDGFR-β blockade**. In preclinical models, sunitinib:

- **Inhibited ligand-dependent RTK phosphorylation** and proliferation of human endothelial cells in response to VEGF, FGF, and PDGF stimulation.
- **Reduced tumor microvessel density** as measured by CD31 immunohistochemical staining.
- **Decreased vascular permeability and blood flow** in dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI studies.
- **Inhibited endothelial cell migration, tubule formation, and induced endothelial cell death** in HUVEC models.

> **Faivre S, Demetri G, Sargent W, Raymond E.** "Molecular basis for sunitinib efficacy and future clinical development." *Nature Reviews Drug Discovery*, 2007; 6: 734–745. DOI: [10.1038/nrd2380](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd2380)

> **Mendel DB, Laird AD, Xin X, et al.** "In vivo antitumor activity of SU11248, a novel tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet-derived growth factor receptors: determination of a pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic relationship." *Clinical Cancer Research*, 2003; 9(1): 327–337. PMID: 12538485.

> **Osusky KL, Hallahan DE, Fu A, et al.** "The receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor SU11248 impedes endothelial cell migration, tubule formation, and blood vessel formation in vivo, but has little effect on existing tumor vessels." *Angiogenesis*, 2004; 7(3): 225–233. DOI: [10.1007/s10456-004-3140-0](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10456-004-3140-0)

> **Hao Z, Sadek I.** "Sunitinib: the antiangiogenic effects and beyond." *OncoTargets and Therapy*, 2016; 9: 5495–5505. DOI: [10.2147/OTT.S112242](https://doi.org/10.2147/OTT.S112242)

> **Christensen JG.** "A preclinical review of sunitinib, a multitargeted receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor with anti-angiogenic and antitumour activities." *Annals of Oncology*, 2007; 18(Suppl 10): x3–x10. DOI: [10.1093/annonc/mdm408](https://doi.org/10.1093/annonc/mdm408)

---

## 2. Anti-Metastatic Roles

### 2.1 Inhibition of Lymphangiogenesis and Lymph Node Metastasis via VEGFR-3

Kodera et al. (2011) demonstrated that sunitinib dually inhibits VEGFR-2 **and** VEGFR-3 signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs), making it one of the first clinically available agents shown to suppress **tumor lymphangiogenesis**. Key findings:

- Sunitinib blocked VEGF-C/D-induced phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3 in LECs (IC₅₀ ~48 nM).
- It abrogated downstream ERK1/2 and Akt activation, attenuating LEC proliferation, migration, and tube formation.
- In an MDA-MB-231LN breast cancer mouse model, sunitinib (40 mg/kg/day) **significantly reduced blood and lymphatic vessel density** and **markedly suppressed axillary lymph node metastasis**, with greater potency than anti-VEGFR-2 antibody (DC101) alone.

> **Kodera Y, Katanasaka Y, Kitamura Y, Tsuda H, Nishio K, Tamura T, Koizumi F.** "Sunitinib inhibits lymphatic endothelial cell functions and lymph node metastasis in a breast cancer model through inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 3." *Breast Cancer Research*, 2011; 13(3): R66. DOI: [10.1186/bcr2903](https://doi.org/10.1186/bcr2903)

### 2.2 Suppression of Distant Metastasis via Reduced Angiogenesis and p-VEGFR-2/p-Tyr

Tanaka et al. (2011) showed that in the highly metastatic BJMC3879 mouse mammary carcinoma model, sunitinib:

- Significantly inhibited tumor growth and **suppressed metastasis to lungs and other visceral organs**.
- Reduced microvessel density and BrdU labeling indices.
- Decreased levels of phosphorylated VEGFR-2 and total phosphotyrosine in primary tumors.
- Notably, lymph node metastasis was **not** significantly reduced, suggesting tissue-specific differences in antimetastatic efficacy.

> **Tanaka Y, Shibata MA, Morimoto J, Otsuki Y.** "Sunitinib suppresses tumor growth and metastases in a highly metastatic mouse mammary cancer model." *Anticancer Research*, 2011; 31(4): 1225–1234. PMID: 21508367.

### 2.3 Antimetastatic Effects via HIF-1α Inhibition in Colorectal Cancer

Yousefian et al. (2025) reported that sunitinib binds favorably to the HIF-1α PAS-B domain and, in hypoxic LoVo colorectal cancer cells:

- Reduced cell migration and invasion.
- Decreased MMP-2 and MMP-9 activity.
- Downregulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) transcription factors.

> **Yousefian et al.** "Exploring the anti-metastatic potential of sunitinib and novel analogs in colorectal cancer: insights into HIF-1α mediated metastasis." *Frontiers in Pharmacology*, 2025; 16: 1520881. DOI: [10.3389/fphar.2025.1520881](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2025.1520881)

### 2.4 Growth Inhibition of Bone Metastases

In a prophylactic bone metastasis model (intracardiac injection of MDA-MB-231 cells), sunitinib inhibited tumor growth in bone and reduced tumor microvessel density (CD34 staining: 63 ± 17 vs 139 ± 11, p < 0.01), though it did not reduce the number of osteolytic lesions or prevent colonization.

> **Mastro et al.** "Preclinical evaluation of Sunitinib as a single agent in the prophylactic setting in a mouse model of bone metastases." *BMC Cancer*, 2013; 13: 32. DOI: [10.1186/1471-2407-13-32](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2407-13-32)

---

## 3. Paradoxical Pro-Metastatic Effects

### 3.1 Acceleration of Metastasis in a Tumor Cell-Type-Dependent Manner via HGF/c-Met

Shojaei et al. (2012) reported that sunitinib, at clinically comparable doses, **increased metastasis** to lung (4T1 breast model) and peritoneal lymph nodes (Colo205 colorectal model), while H460 lung tumors showed no increased invasiveness, indicating tumor cell-type dependence. Mechanistically:

- Sunitinib-induced hypoxia upregulated HGF from stromal cells, activating tumor cell c-Met in a paracrine manner.
- Crizotinib (dual c-Met/ALK inhibitor) combined with sunitinib **reduced metastasis in all models**, confirming c-Met as a key mediator of sunitinib-induced metastasis.

> **Shojaei F, Simmons BH, Lee JH, Lappin PB, Christensen JG.** "HGF/c-Met pathway is one of the mediators of sunitinib-induced tumor cell type-dependent metastasis." *Cancer Letters*, 2012; 320(1): 48–55. DOI: [10.1016/j.canlet.2012.01.026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.canlet.2012.01.026)

The upstream mechanism was established by Sennino et al. (2012), showing that VEGF-pathway inhibition (including sunitinib) in RIP-Tag2 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors causes vascular pruning → hypoxia → HIF-1α accumulation → c-Met activation → increased invasion and liver metastasis. Concurrent c-Met inhibition blocked these effects.

> **Sennino B, Ishiguro-Oonuma T, Wei Y, et al.** "Suppression of tumor invasion and metastasis by concurrent inhibition of c-Met and VEGF signaling in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors." *Cancer Discovery*, 2012; 2(3): 270–287. DOI: [10.1158/2159-8290.CD-11-0240](https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-11-0240)

### 3.2 Endothelial Cell Senescence and Pre-Metastatic Niche Formation

Wang et al. (2020) provided a distinct mechanistic explanation: sunitinib induces a **senescence-like phenotype in endothelial cells (ECs)**, leading to:

- Increased secretion of inflammatory chemokines and upregulation of VCAM1, promoting tumor cell chemotaxis and EC adhesion.
- Downregulation of VE-cadherin, loosening EC junctions and facilitating tumor cell transmigration.
- Recruitment of cancer-associated myeloid cells (neutrophils, macrophages) forming a "pre-metastatic niche" in distant organs.
- Ultimately, increased lung metastasis in the 4T1 breast cancer model.

> **Wang D, Xiao F, Feng Z, et al.** "Sunitinib facilitates metastatic breast cancer spreading by inducing endothelial cell senescence." *Breast Cancer Research*, 2020; 22: 103. DOI: [10.1186/s13058-020-01346-y](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13058-020-01346-y)

### 3.3 Dose- and Model-Dependent Contrasting Effects

Preece/Welch et al. (2012) systematically compared 4T1 (breast) and RENCA (renal) lung metastasis models and found:

- **High-dose sunitinib** (120 mg/kg) prior to tumor cell injection **promoted** 4T1 lung metastasis seeding via pericyte depletion in the lung vasculature.
- **Clinically relevant doses** did not promote metastasis.
- After tumor cell injection, sunitinib **suppressed** RENCA metastases but **failed to suppress** 4T1 metastases (the latter associated with persistent vascularization and Gr1+CD11b+ myeloid cell recruitment).
- Thus, the metastatic response to sunitinib is **dose-dependent**, **tumor model-dependent**, and influenced by myeloid cell-mediated resistance.

> **Preece N (Welch et al.).** "Contrasting effects of sunitinib within in vivo models of metastasis." *Angiogenesis*, 2012; 15: 623–641. DOI: [10.1007/s10456-012-9291-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10456-012-9291-z)
