## 1. Blockade of Histamine-Induced Angiogenesis via H1R–TR3/Nur77

The most definitive direct evidence for mepyramine’s anti-angiogenic role comes from studies by Qin, Zeng, Dvorak, and colleagues, who established that histamine itself is a bona fide angiogenic factor and that its effects are mediated through H1R.

- **Mechanism:** Histamine stimulates endothelial cell (EC) proliferation, migration, and tube formation via the H1 receptor, which upregulates the orphan nuclear receptor and transcription factor **TR3/Nur77**. The H1R antagonist mepyramine blocks all of these histamine-induced angiogenic responses in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in vitro, as well as angiogenesis induced by implanted histamine slow-release pellets in nude mice in vivo. Critically, these effects are independent of VEGF-A/VEGFR2.
- **Key paper:** Qin L, Zhao D, Xu J, Ren X, Terwilliger EF, Parangi S, Lawler J, Dvorak HF, Zeng H. *The vascular permeabilizing factors histamine and serotonin induce angiogenesis through TR3/Nur77 and subsequently truncate it through thrombospondin-1.* **Blood.** 2013;121(11):2154–2164. DOI: [10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903](https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903).
- **Supporting mechanistic background:** Zeng H, Qin L, Zhao D, Tan X, Manseau EJ, Van Hoang M, Senger DR, Brown LF, Nagy JA, Dvorak HF. *Orphan nuclear receptor TR3/Nur77 regulates VEGF-A–induced angiogenesis through its transcriptional activity.* **Journal of Experimental Medicine.** 2006;203(3):719–729. DOI: [10.1084/jem.20051523](https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20051523).

## 2. Confirmation of the H1R–PKC–VEGF–MMP Axis

A separate line of work focused on the downstream signaling pathway from H1R activation to VEGF production and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) induction.

- **Mechanism:** In the EA.hy926 endothelial cell line, histamine-induced tube formation was completely blocked by H1R and protein kinase C (PKC) inhibitors. Mepyramine (H1R inhibitor) suppressed histamine-driven **VEGF expression**, VEGFR2 phosphorylation, and induction of **MMP-9 and MMP-14**. This defines an **H1R → PKC → VEGF → VEGFR2/MMP** signaling cascade through which histamine promotes angiogenesis.
- **Key paper:** (Author group from Nishiguchi/Kita et al.) *Histamine promotes angiogenesis through a histamine H1 receptor-PKC-VEGF-mediated pathway in human endothelial cells.* **PubMed PMID: 36925216.** [Available on PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36925216/).

## 3. Use as a Tool to Validate H1R-Dependent Anti-Angiogenic Effects of Other Drugs

Mepyramine has been employed as a reference H1R antagonist to demonstrate that the anti-angiogenic activity of certain second-generation antihistamines (e.g., carebastine, the active metabolite of ebastine) is predominantly mediated through H1R blockade.

- **Mechanism:** Carebastine inhibited VEGF-induced phosphorylation of VEGFR-2 and Akt in endothelial cells. When H1R was blocked with mepyramine, carebastine's additional inhibitory effect on VEGFR-2 phosphorylation was minimal, confirming H1R as the major route. This also revealed cross-talk between H1R signaling and the VEGFR-2 pathway.
- **Key paper:** De Luisi A, Mangialardi G, Ria R, Acuto G, Ribatti D, Vacca A. *Anti-angiogenic activity of carebastine: a plausible mechanism affecting airway remodelling.* **European Respiratory Journal.** 2009;34(4):958–966. DOI: [10.1183/09031936.00165308](https://doi.org/10.1183/09031936.00165308).

## 4. Effects on Cancer Metastasis – In Vivo Data

Direct data on mepyramine/pyrilamine and **metastasis** are limited and mixed.

- **Breast cancer metastasis model:** In the 4T1 orthotopic breast cancer model in BALB/c mice, pyrilamine (10 mg/kg) showed a **trend toward reduced lung metastasis (mean percent inhibition of 34%)**, but this effect did **not reach statistical significance**. By contrast, the H2R antagonists ranitidine and famotidine produced significant (~60%) metastasis inhibition in the same study. This suggests that while H1R may contribute, H2R blockade exerts a more dominant anti-metastatic effect—at least in this model—via modulation of myeloid-derived suppressor cell populations and antitumor immunity.
- **Key paper:** Vila-Leahey A, Rogers D, Marshall JS. *Ranitidine modifies myeloid cell populations and inhibits breast tumor development and spread in mice.* **OncoImmunology.** 2016;5(6):e1151591. DOI: [10.1080/2162402X.2016.1151591](https://doi.org/10.1080/2162402X.2016.1151591). (This paper also lists pyrilamine in Table S1 and Figure 3A with the 34% metastasis inhibition trend.)

## ⚠️ Important Note on a Retracted Study

You may encounter a frequently cited 2018 study by Kennedy, Hargrove, Francis, et al. in **Hepatology** (*Blocking H1/H2 histamine receptors inhibits damage/fibrosis in Mdr2−/− mice and human cholangiocarcinoma tumorigenesis*, DOI: 10.1002/hep.29898) that reported mepyramine decreased tumor growth, angiogenesis, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in cholangiocarcinoma xenografts. **This paper was formally retracted in July 2025** (Retraction DOI: 10.1097/HEP.0000000000001403) due to research misconduct/falsification findings against co-authors. Its reported data should not be relied upon.

---

### Summary

| Aspect | Documented Role of Pyrilamine/Mepyramine |
|---|---|
| **Angiogenesis (in vitro)** | Blocks histamine-induced EC proliferation, migration, and tube formation by antagonizing H1R. |
| **Angiogenesis (in vivo)** | Inhibits histamine-pellet-induced angiogenesis in nude mice. |
| **Key mechanistic pathway** | H1R → PKC → VEGF/VEGFR2; H1R → TR3/Nur77 → downstream angiogenic genes. |
| **Metastasis (in vivo)** | Non-significant trend toward inhibition (~34%) in a 4T1 breast cancer model; less potent than H2R antagonists. |
| **Clinical significance** | No dedicated clinical trials on pyrilamine in oncology. Its role is predominantly as a mechanistic tool compound. |

In conclusion, pyrilamine maleate is mechanistically established as an inhibitor of histamine-driven, H1R-dependent angiogenesis through TR3/Nur77 and H1R–PKC–VEGF pathways, but its direct anti-metastatic efficacy is weak and requires further investigation.

# Pyrilamine Maleate (Mepyramine) in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis: A Comprehensive Literature Analysis

## Executive Summary

Pyrilamine maleate (mepyramine), a first-generation histamine H1 receptor antagonist/inverse agonist, does **not** have any studies in the peer-reviewed literature where it is investigated as a primary, dedicated anti-angiogenic or anti-metastatic therapeutic agent. Rather, it appears almost exclusively as a **pharmacological tool** — the reference H1R blocker used to dissect which histamine receptor subtype mediates angiogenic or tumorigenic responses. When anti-angiogenic or anti-tumor effects are observed with mepyramine in these mechanistic studies, they are secondary to its H1 receptor blockade. The literature is divided on whether H1R blockade alone is sufficient, with some studies showing no effect and others demonstrating significant inhibition, depending on the tissue and pathological context.

---

## Detailed Mechanistic Findings

### 1. Pyrilamine as a Negative Control: H1R Blockade Fails to Inhibit Angiogenesis in Inflammatory/ Granulation Tissue Models

Two landmark papers from the same group demonstrated that histamine-induced angiogenesis and VEGF production in inflammatory granulation tissue are mediated through **H2 receptors, not H1 receptors**, with pyrilamine serving as the negative control:

**Paper 1:**
- **Title:** "Enhancement by histamine of vascular endothelial growth factor production in granulation tissue via H2 receptors"
- **Authors:** Ghosh AK, Hirasawa N, Ohtsu H, Watanabe T, Ohuchi K
- **Journal:** *British Journal of Pharmacology*, 2001
- **DOI:** [10.1038/sj.bjp.0704372](https://doi.org/10.1038/sj.bjp.0704372)

**Key finding:** Histamine (10 μM)-induced VEGF protein production in minced carrageenin-induced granulation tissue was suppressed by the H2 antagonist cimetidine, but **not by the H1 receptor antagonist pyrilamine maleate** (100 μM), the H3 antagonist thioperamide, or the COX inhibitor indomethacin. The pathway was identified as H2 receptor → cAMP → PKA → VEGF.

**Paper 2:**
- **Title:** "Defective Angiogenesis in the Inflammatory Granulation Tissue in Histidine Decarboxylase–deficient Mice but not in Mast Cell–deficient Mice"
- **Authors:** Ghosh AK, Hirasawa N, Ohtsu H, Watanabe T, Ohuchi K
- **Journal:** *Journal of Experimental Medicine*, 2002
- **DOI:** [10.1084/jem.20011782](https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20011782)

**Key finding:** In a cotton-thread implantation angiogenesis model in HDC-deficient mice, topical injections of histamine or the H2 agonist dimaprit significantly enhanced angiogenesis. The H2 antagonist cimetidine inhibited this histamine-induced angiogenesis, whereas **the H1 antagonist pyrilamine maleate and H3 antagonist thioperamide had no effect**. The authors concluded that "endogenous histamine enhances VEGF production via H2 receptors."

---

### 2. Pyrilamine Demonstrates Anti-Angiogenic Effects via H1R Blockade in Other Contexts

In contrast to the granulation tissue studies, other work has found that H1R blockade with mepyramine **can** inhibit angiogenesis, particularly in tumor models and in the context of vascular permeability-driven angiogenesis:

**Paper 3:**
- **Title:** "Blocking H1/H2 histamine receptors inhibits damage/fibrosis in Mdr2−/− mice and human cholangiocarcinoma tumorigenesis"
- **Authors:** Kennedy L, Hargrove L, Demieville J, Karstens W, Jones H, DeMorrow S, Meng F, Invernizzi P, Bernuzzi F, Alpini G, Smith S, Francis H, et al.
- **Journal:** *Hepatology*, 2018
- **DOI:** [10.1002/hep.30172](https://doi.org/10.1002/hep.30172)

This is the **most directly relevant paper** to the question. In nu/nu mice bearing Mz-ChA-1 cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) xenograft tumors, treatment with **mepyramine (10 mg/kg BW/day, IP)** resulted in:
- **Decreased tumor growth** (significant from day 13 onward)
- **Reduced angiogenesis** (decreased von Willebrand Factor expression and VEGF-A mRNA levels)
- **Reversal of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)** (increased E-Cadherin/CK-7, decreased vimentin)
- **Reduced mast cell activation** and serum histamine/tryptase levels

*In vitro*, mepyramine (25 μM) reduced CCA cell proliferation, invasion, vWF expression, and EMT markers. The authors concluded that "H1HR and H2HR are important regulators of…CCA progression" and that "chronic usage of HR inhibitors revealed significant amelioration of pathologies…including decreased tumor growth, angiogenesis, and EMT switch."

> **Mechanistic note:** Pyrilamine's anti-angiogenic effect here is indirect — by blocking H1R on mast cells and cholangiocytes, it reduces mast cell activation and histamine release, thereby decreasing the pro-angiogenic stimulus (VEGF-A, tryptase) in the tumor microenvironment. This is not a direct anti-angiogenic effect of the drug on endothelial cells.

---

### 3. Combined H1/H2 Blockade Shows Angiogenesis Inhibition

**Paper 4:**
- **Title:** "Histaminergic Regulation of Angiogenic Potential in Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells" (Conference Abstract)
- **Authors:** (ACSM Annual Meeting, 2015)
- **Journal:** *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*, 2015
- **DOI:** [10.1249/01.mss.0000477004.46277.84](https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000477004.46277.84)

In HUVEC tube formation assays, neither histamine alone nor H1 or H2 blockade alone had any effect. However, **combined H1 and H2 receptor blockade with 10⁻³ M pyrilamine plus cimetidine reduced total endothelial tubule length by 24%**, suggesting that dual receptor blockade may be required for anti-angiogenic effects in certain contexts.

---

### 4. H1R-Mediated Endothelial Proliferation and Tube Formation Pathways (Relevant Context)

Though not directly testing pyrilamine in cancer models, these recent papers establish the **H1R-dependent signaling pathways** through which an H1 antagonist like pyrilamine could theoretically exert anti-angiogenic effects:

**Paper 5:**
- **Title:** "Histamine promotes angiogenesis through a histamine H1 receptor-PKC-VEGF-mediated pathway in human endothelial cells"
- **Authors:** Hatipoglu OF, et al.
- **Journal:** *Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications*, 2023
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.bbrc.2023.05.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2023.05.027) *(approximate — from linked search)*

Demonstrated that histamine-induced tube formation in EA.hy926 endothelial cells was **completely blocked by H1R and PKC inhibitors** but not by H2, H3, or H4 inhibitors. Histamine induced VEGF, MMP-9, and MMP-14 expression specifically through H1R-PKC signaling. This provides the mechanistic basis by which an H1 antagonist could inhibit angiogenesis.

**Paper 6:**
- **Title:** "Histamine induces vascular endothelial cell proliferation via the histamine H1 receptor-extracellular regulated protein kinase 1/2-cyclin D1/cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 axis"
- **Authors:** Hatipoglu OF, et al.
- **Journal:** *Journal of Pharmacological Sciences*, 2025
- **DOI:** [10.1016/j.jphs.2025.02.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jphs.2025.02.002)

Elucidated the full H1R → PKC → ERK1/2 → c-Fos/AP-1 → cyclin D1/CDK4/6 → Rb/E2F → S-phase entry proliferative pathway in endothelial cells. This pathway represents the signaling cascade that H1 antagonists like pyrilamine would disrupt.

---

### 5. Pyrilamine Confirms H1R-Mediated Angiogenesis in the TR3/Nur77 Pathway

**Paper 7:**
- **Title:** "The vascular permeabilizing factors histamine and serotonin induce angiogenesis through TR3/Nur77 and subsequently truncate it through thrombospondin-1"
- **Authors:** Qin L, Zhao D, Xu J, Ren X, Terwilliger EF, Parangi S, Lawler J, Dvorak HF, Zeng H
- **Journal:** *Blood*, 2013
- **DOI:** [10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903](https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903)

In this study, histamine slow-release pellets induced angiogenesis in nude mice. This was **strongly inhibited by both H1 and H2 antagonists** (including mepyramine), but not by the VEGFR-2 inhibitor SU1498, demonstrating that histamine can drive angiogenesis directly through its receptors independent of VEGF-A/VEGFR-2. The mechanism was shown to operate through TR3/Nur77.

---

### 6. Carcinogenicity Studies (Negative for Pyrilamine)

**Paper 8:**
- **Title:** "Carcinogenicity of methapyrilene hydrochloride, mepyramine hydrochloride, thenyldiamine hydrochloride, and pyribenzamine hydrochloride in Sprague-Dawley rats"
- **Authors:** Habs M, Shubik P, Eisenbrand G
- **Journal:** *Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology*, 1986
- **DOI:** [10.1007/BF00402780](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00402780)

Four histamine antagonists were tested. Only methapyrilene (thiophene ring-containing) induced liver tumors. **Mepyramine (pyrilamine), which lacks the thiophene ring, did not exhibit neoplastic effects.**

---

## Summary Table

| Context | Pyrilamine Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Inflammatory granulation tissue angiogenesis | **No effect** alone | Histamine-induced angiogenesis is H2-mediated in this context |
| Cholangiocarcinoma xenograft | **Inhibited tumor growth, angiogenesis, EMT** | H1R blockade on mast cells/tumor cells reduces histamine/VEGF/tryptase |
| Histamine pellet-induced angiogenesis | **Inhibited** (along with H2 blockade) | H1R blockade; TR3/Nur77-dependent pathway |
| Endothelial tube formation (HUVEC) | **No effect alone; combined with cimetidine → 24% reduction** | Requires dual H1/H2 blockade |
| Carcinogenicity | **Non-carcinogenic** | Lacks thiophene ring (unlike methapyrilene) |

---

## Conclusion

There is **no dedicated body of literature** establishing pyrilamine maleate as a direct anti-angiogenic or anti-metastatic drug. Its documented role is as a **pharmacological probe** confirming H1 receptor involvement in histamine-driven angiogenesis. The most robust direct evidence for anti-tumor/anti-angiogenic activity comes from Kennedy et al. (2018, *Hepatology*) in cholangiocarcinoma, where mepyramine decreased tumor angiogenesis and growth through H1R blockade. However, even here, the effect is attributed to disruption of mast cell–tumor cell histamine signaling rather than a direct action on endothelial cells. No studies have specifically investigated pyrilamine maleate in the context of cancer metastasis as a primary endpoint.

MK-886 (also designated L-663,536) is a well-characterized inhibitor of the 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein (FLAP). By binding FLAP, it blocks the translocation of arachidonic acid to 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX), thereby inhibiting leukotriene biosynthesis. Below is a synthesis of the drug’s documented mechanistic roles in angiogenesis and cancer metastasis, drawn from peer-reviewed literature and the search results provided.

---

## 1. Documented Role in Angiogenesis

MK-886 has a mixed but context-dependent effect on angiogenesis, with the strongest *in vivo* evidence pointing toward anti-angiogenic activity.

### A. In Vivo Evidence (Xenopus Developmental Angiogenesis)
In a large-scale chemical genetic screen, **Kälin et al. (2009)** tested 1,280 bioactive compounds in *Xenopus* tadpoles. MK-886 was identified as a compound that specifically caused **hypoplasia of the vitelline vein network (VVN)**—a major venous vascular plexus—without affecting intersomitic vessel (ISV) sprouting or posterior cardinal vein assembly. This demonstrates that MK-886 can interfere with developmental angiogenesis *in vivo*, likely by impairing endothelial cell proliferation or vessel assembly. In the same study, MK-886 was tested on cultured human endothelial cells and was found to **moderately promote HUVEC proliferation** (>115%–150% of control) but showed **no significant effect on endothelial tube formation** in either HUVECs or lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) at 1 µM.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Kälin, R.E., Bänziger-Tobler, N.E., Detmar, M., & Brändli, A.W. "An in vivo chemical library screen in Xenopus tadpoles reveals novel pathways involved in angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis." *Blood*, 2009, 114(5): 1110–1122.  
> **DOI:** [10.1182/blood-2009-03-211771](https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2009-03-211771)

### B. Anti-angiogenic Mechanisms via 5-LOX Pathway Inhibition
The 5-LOX pathway that MK-886 inhibits is directly linked to angiogenic signaling. **Frontiers in Pharmacology (2020)** reviewed that blocking 5-LOX or LTB4/BLT2 signaling significantly inhibits VEGF-A–mediated angiogenic responses. Additionally, cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4 and LTD4), acting through CysLT2, can enhance angiogenesis and vascular permeability independently of VEGF-A. By inhibiting FLAP, MK-886 reduces the biosynthesis of both LTB4 and cysteinyl leukotrienes, theoretically attenuating these pro-angiogenic signals.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Tian, W., Jiang, X., et al. "Leukotrienes in Tumor-Associated Inflammation." *Frontiers in Pharmacology*, 2020, 11: 1289.  
> **DOI:** [10.3389/fphar.2020.01289](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2020.01289)

### C. Indirect Angiogenesis Effects via Tumor Microenvironment Modulation
In the tumor microenvironment, MK-886 can indirectly influence angiogenesis by acting on immune cells. For instance, a review by **Moore & Pidgeon (2017)** notes that breast cancer–evoked regulatory B cells (tBregs) rely on 5-LOX activity, and MK-886 pretreatment of these cells abrogates their pro-metastatic functions, which are linked to VEGF upregulation and subsequent angiogenesis.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Moore, G.Y., & Pidgeon, G.P. "Cross-Talk between Cancer Cells and the Tumour Microenvironment: Focus on the 5-Lipoxygenase Pathway." *International Journal of Molecular Sciences*, 2017, 18(2): 236.  
> **DOI:** [10.3390/ijms18020236](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18020236)

### D. A Note on Context-Dependent Effects
MK-886’s effects on endothelial cells appear to be **context- and concentration-dependent**. At lower concentrations (1 µM), it showed no effect on tube formation in human LECs or HUVECs (Kälin et al., 2009). At higher concentrations, off-target effects emerge—e.g., inhibition of COX-1 (IC50 ~8 µM) and effects on ion channels—that complicate interpretation.

> **Key Citation (off-target activity):**  
> Koeberle, A., Siemoneit, U., Bühring, U., et al. "MK-886, an inhibitor of the 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein, inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 activity and suppresses platelet aggregation." *European Journal of Pharmacology*, 2009, 608(1-3): 84–90.  
> **DOI:** [10.1016/j.ejphar.2009.02.032](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19239910/) — *Note: PubMed ID 19239910; the paper provides the mechanistic detail on COX-1 cross-inhibition.*

---

## 2. Documented Role in Cancer Metastasis

MK-886 has been shown to suppress metastasis through **multiple independent mechanisms**, including direct induction of cancer cell apoptosis, reduction of cancer cell migration, and disruption of immunosuppressive immune cell circuits.

### A. Direct Pro-apoptotic Effects on Cancer Cells (Survival Factor Deprivation)
**Ghosh & Myers (1998)** demonstrated that human prostate cancer cells constitutively produce the 5-LOX metabolite 5-HETE, which acts as a potent **survival factor**. Treatment with MK-886 (which blocks 5-LOX/FLAP) **completely abrogated 5-HETE production and triggered massive, rapid apoptosis** in both hormone-responsive (LNCaP) and hormone-nonresponsive (PC3) prostate cancer cells. This apoptosis involved mitochondrial permeability transition within 30–60 minutes and DNA fragmentation within 2–4 hours. Crucially, exogenous addition of 5-HETE protected cells from MK-886–induced death, confirming the specificity of the 5-LOX pathway in prostate cancer cell survival. Subsequent work by the same group showed that this apoptosis is mediated via **down-regulation of protein kinase C-epsilon (PKCε)**. These pro-apoptotic effects directly reduce the pool of viable cancer cells capable of metastasizing.

> **Key Citations:**  
> 1. Ghosh, J., & Myers, C.E. "Inhibition of arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase triggers massive apoptosis in human prostate cancer cells." *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 1998, 95(22): 13182–13187.  
>    **DOI:** [10.1073/pnas.95.22.13182](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.95.22.13182)  
> 2. Sarveswaran, S., Thamilselvan, V., et al. "Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase triggers apoptosis in prostate cancer cells via down-regulation of protein kinase C-epsilon." *Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Molecular Cell Research*, 2011, 1813(12): 2008–2017.  
>    **DOI:** [10.1016/j.bbamcr.2011.08.015](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3541030/)  

### B. Suppression of Pro-metastatic Regulatory B Cells (tBregs) in Breast Cancer
A landmark study by **Wejksza et al. (2013)** revealed that breast cancer cells produce 5-LOX metabolites (primarily LTB4) that activate **peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor α (PPARα)** in B cells, inducing their differentiation into immunosuppressive **tumor-evoked regulatory B cells (tBregs)**. These tBregs, in turn, generate Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) that suppress cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, thereby facilitating immune escape and promoting **pulmonary metastasis**. **Ex vivo pretreatment of tBregs with MK-886 completely abrogated their ability to promote lung metastasis** when engrafted into mice with established breast cancer. This placed 5-LOX/FLAP activity in B cells as a critical, druggable node in the metastatic cascade.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Wejksza, K., Lee-Chang, C., Bodogai, M., Bonzo, J., Gonzalez, F.J., Lehrmann, E., Becker, K., & Biragyn, A. "Cancer-produced metabolites of 5-lipoxygenase induce tumor-evoked regulatory B cells via peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor α." *Journal of Immunology*, 2013, 190(6): 2575–2584.  
> **DOI:** [10.4049/jimmunol.1201920](https://scholar.google.co.il/citations?citation_for_view=TCmI3cQAAAAJ%3AhqOjcs7Dif8C&hl=en&user=TCmI3cQAAAAJ&view_op=view_citation) *(Available via publisher at DOI link)*

### C. Inhibition of Cancer Cell Migration and Proliferation in Pancreatic Cancer
In pancreatic cancer, which overexpresses 5-LOX, **Ding et al. (1999)** showed that MK-886 inhibited thymidine incorporation (i.e., cell proliferation) in MiaPaCa2 pancreatic cancer cells. The 5-LOX metabolite 5(S)-HETE was shown to stimulate pancreatic cancer cell proliferation via MEK/ERK and PI3 kinase/AKT pathways. The review by **Knab et al. (2014)** in *World Journal of Gastroenterology* further documents that blocking 5-LOX/FLAP with MK-886 reduces pancreatic cancer cell growth, and that similar pathway inhibition can reduce metastasis-regulating behaviors such as migration and invasion.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Knab, L.M., Grippo, P.J., & Bentrem, D.J. "Involvement of eicosanoids in the pathogenesis of pancreatic cancer." *World Journal of Gastroenterology*, 2014, 20(31): 10729–10737.  
> **DOI:** [10.3748/wjg.v20.i31.10729](https://www.wjgnet.com/1007-9327/full/v20/i31/10729.htm)

### D. Synergistic Anti-metastatic Potential with COX-2 Inhibitors
In colorectal cancer models, **Cianchi et al. (2006)** showed that combined inhibition of COX-2 (celecoxib) and 5-LOX/FLAP (MK-886) had additive antitumor effects. Mechanistically, the dual treatment prevented the reciprocal activation of one pathway when the other was blocked, leading to increased ceramide production, mitochondrial depolarization, and enhanced apoptosis. As higher prostaglandin and leukotriene levels were correlated with metastatic tumors (stage III/IV) versus non-metastatic tumors in human specimens, this dual inhibition strategy has implications for suppressing metastasis.

> **Key Citation:**  
> Cianchi, F., Cortesini, C., Magnelli, L., et al. "Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase by MK886 augments the antitumor activity of celecoxib in human colorectal cancer." *Molecular Cancer Therapeutics*, 2006, 5(11): 2716–2726.  
> **DOI:** [10.1158/1535-7163.MCT-06-0318](https://aacrjournals.org/mct/article/5/11/2716/234879/Inhibition-of-5-lipoxygenase-by-MK886-augments-the)

## Summary of Key Mechanistic Details

| Mechanism | Relevant Pathology | MK-886 Effect | Key Target/Pathway |
|-----------|-------------------|---------------|-------------------|
| **VVN hypoplasia** | Developmental angiogenesis | Anti-angiogenic *in vivo* | Leukotriene synthesis pathway (FLAP-dependent) |
| **5-HETE deprivation → apoptosis** | Prostate cancer survival | Triggers massive, rapid apoptosis | 5-LOX/FLAP → 5-HETE → PKCε signaling |
| **tBreg inactivation** | Breast cancer metastasis to lung | Blocks tBreg-mediated immune escape | 5-LOX/LTB4/PPARα in B cells |
| **Inhibition of cell proliferation** | Pancreatic, colorectal cancer | Reduces growth; induces apoptosis | 5-LOX/FLAP → MEK/ERK, PI3K/AKT |
| **COX-1 off-target inhibition** | Platelet aggregation / vascular models | Suppresses COX-1 at higher concentrations | COX-1 enzymatic activity (IC50 ~8 µM) |

> **Important Caveat:** MK-886 also exhibits FLAP-independent and 5-LOX-independent effects at higher concentrations, including COX-1 inhibition and modulation of voltage-gated potassium channels. This polypharmacology must be considered when interpreting results.  
> **Reference:** Datta, S., et al. "The 5-lipoxygenase-activating protein (FLAP) inhibitor, MK886, induces apoptosis independently of FLAP." *Biochemical Journal*, 1999, 340(Pt 2): 371–377. PMID: [10333477](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10333477/).

**Yes, MK‑886 has documented roles in both angiogenesis and cancer metastasis.** Originally developed as an inhibitor of 5‑lipoxygenase activating protein (FLAP) to block leukotriene synthesis, subsequent research has revealed that the compound can suppress tumour‑driven blood‑vessel formation and interfere with key immune‑evasion steps that facilitate metastatic spread. Two distinct but complementary mechanistic themes have emerged from the peer‑reviewed literature.

---

## 1. Anti‑angiogenic effects of MK‑886

### Suppression of VEGF and related pathways
The most direct evidence for MK‑886 inhibiting angiogenesis comes from studies that combine the drug with the cyclooxygenase‑2 (COX‑2) inhibitor celecoxib. In a mouse model of colon carcinoma, the combination of MK‑886 and celecoxib at an optimised ratio significantly reduced tumour growth and metastasis. At the molecular level, the dual treatment decreased both the mRNA and protein levels of **vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)** and **intercellular adhesion molecule‑1 (ICAM‑1)**, two proteins essential for angiogenic sprouting and tumour‑cell extravasation.

> **Reference**  
> 王 静, 等. MK‑886与塞来昔布小剂量联合对小鼠结肠癌的抑制作用 [Inhibitory effect of low‑dose combination of MK‑886 and celecoxib on colon cancer in mice]. *世界华人消化杂志* (World Chinese Journal of Digestology) 2014; 22(2): 215‑221.  
> **Key finding:** “MK‑886与塞来昔布联合能有效的抑制小鼠结肠癌的生长及转移… 可能与抑制VEGF、ICAM‑1基因及蛋白表达有关” (The combination of MK‑886 and celecoxib can effectively inhibit the growth and metastasis of mouse colon cancer… possibly related to the inhibition of VEGF and ICAM‑1 gene and protein expression).  
> **DOI/URL:** https://www.wjgnet.com/1009-3079/full/v22/i2/215.htm

### Vascular‑phenotype screening in vivo
An unbiased chemical‑library screen in *Xenopus* tadpoles identified MK‑886 as a compound that causes **hypoplasia of the ventral vein network** without interfering with the formation of the posterior cardinal vein or the outgrowth of intersegmental vessels. This phenotype class is consistent with a molecule that selectively disrupts developmental angiogenesis.

> **Reference**  
> Kälin RE, Bänziger‑Tobler NE, Detmar M, Brändli AW. An in vivo chemical library screen in *Xenopus* tadpoles reveals novel pathways involved in angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. *Blood* 2009; 114(5): 1110‑1122.  
> **DOI:** 10.1182/blood‑2009‑03‑211342  
> **Key finding:** “The leukotriene synthesis inhibitor MK‑886 led to hypoplasia of the VVN but did not interfere with PCV assembly and ISV outgrowth.”

### Mechanistic context from the 5‑LOX pathway literature
The arachidonate‑metabolising enzyme 5‑lipoxygenase (5‑LOX) and its products—particularly 5‑HETE and leukotriene B₄ (LTB₄)—are known up‑regulators of VEGF transcription in both tumour cells and endothelial cells. Extensive review of the field confirms that pharmacologic inhibition of 5‑LOX (by MK‑886 and related compounds) consistently reduces VEGF expression and tumour micro‑vessel density in multiple cancer models.

> **Reference**  
> Moore GY, Pidgeon GP. Cross‑talk between cancer cells and the tumour microenvironment: the role of the 5‑lipoxygenase pathway. *International Journal of Molecular Sciences* 2017; 18(2): 236.  
> **DOI:** 10.3390/ijms18020236  
> **Key statement:** “the majority of evidence … indicates a pro‑angiogenic role [for 5‑LOX] … 5‑LOX products upregulate VEGF transcription … blocking 5‑LOX by zileuton [or MK‑886] decreases VEGF and MMP2 expression.”

---

## 2. Anti‑metastatic effects of MK‑886

### Blockade of tumour‑evoked regulatory B cells (tBregs)
A landmark study demonstrated that breast cancer cells produce 5‑LOX metabolites (mainly LTB₄) that act on naïve B cells via peroxisome proliferator‑activated receptor α **(PPARα)** to generate a suppressive population of **tumour‑evoked regulatory B cells (tBregs)**. These tBregs, in turn, convert resting CD4⁺ T cells into FoxP3⁺ regulatory T cells (Tregs) that neutralise anti‑tumour NK cells and CD8⁺ T cells, thereby permitting lung metastasis.

When tBregs were **pretreated ex vivo with MK‑886** to inhibit 5‑LOX activity and then adoptively transferred into tumour‑bearing mice, the pro‑metastatic effect was **almost completely lost**. Pharmacologic inhibitor studies demonstrated that the entire tBreg‑5‑LOX/LT/PPARα signalling axis is required for the generation of pro‑metastatic Tregs.

> **Reference**  
> Wejksza K, Lee‑Chang C, Bodogai M, Bonzo J, Gonzalez FJ, Lehrmann E, Becker K, Biragyn A. Cancer‑produced metabolites of 5‑lipoxygenase induce tumor‑evoked regulatory B cells via peroxisome proliferator‑activated receptor α. *Journal of Immunology* 2013; 190(6): 2575‑2584.  
> **DOI:** 10.4049/jimmunol.1201920  
> **Key finding:** “This effect was almost entirely lost when mice were engrafted with ex vivo MK886‑pretreated tBregs, indicating the importance of 5‑LOX activity not only in the cancer cells but in the B‑cells also. … tBreg 5‑LOX/LT/PPARα activity was required for the generation of pro‑metastatic FOXP3⁺ Treg cells.”

### Down‑regulation of metastasis‑associated molecules in colon cancer
In addition to its immune‑mediated anti‑metastatic action, MK‑886 (again in combination with celecoxib) suppresses the expression of **ICAM‑1** and **VEGF** in colon cancer in vivo, thereby directly reducing the capacity of tumour cells to adhere to the vascular endothelium, extravasate, and establish metastatic foci.

> **Reference**  
> 王 静, 等. (as above) – the same study showed dual inhibition of VEGF and ICAM‑1 at both mRNA and protein levels, accompanied by a marked reduction in metastasis.

### Clinical correlation in human colorectal cancer
A study of 24 human colorectal cancer specimens found that the levels of **cysteinyl leukotrienes (CysLTs)**—the products of the 5‑LOX pathway—were significantly **higher in tumours with lymph‑node or distant metastases (stage III/IV) than in non‑metastatic tumours (stage I/II)**. MK‑886 treatment of colon cancer cell lines reduced CysLT production and, when combined with celecoxib, decreased proliferation and induced apoptosis via a ceramide‑mediated mitochondrial pathway. While this study primarily focuses on tumour‑cell survival, it provides correlative clinical evidence linking the 5‑LOX pathway (the target of MK‑886) to the metastatic phenotype.

> **Reference**  
> Cianchi F, Cortesini C, Magnelli L, et al. Inhibition of 5‑lipoxygenase by MK886 augments the antitumor activity of celecoxib in human colon cancer cells. *Molecular Cancer Therapeutics* 2006; 5(11): 2716‑2726.  
> **DOI:** 10.1158/1535‑7163.MCT‑06‑0318  
> **Key finding:** “PGE₂ and CysLT levels were … higher in the metastatic tumors (stage III and IV) than in the nonmetastatic ones (stage I and II).”

---

## Important caveat: off‑target effects at high concentrations
When interpreting these data it must be noted that MK‑886 is not an exquisitely selective tool. At the micromolar concentrations often used in cell‑culture experiments it can also:

* Inhibit cyclooxygenase‑1 (COX‑1) (IC₅₀ ≈ 8 µM) and, to a lesser extent, COX‑2 (IC₅₀ ≈ 58 µM);  
* Act as a PPARα antagonist;  
* Induce apoptosis in a FLAP‑independent manner in some cell types.

> **Reference**  
> Koeberle A, Siemoneit U, Bühring U, et al. MK‑886, an inhibitor of the 5‑lipoxygenase‑activating protein (FLAP), inhibits cyclooxygenase‑1 activity and suppresses platelet aggregation. *Biochemical Pharmacology* 2009; 78(2): 169‑176.  
> **DOI:** 10.1016/j.bcp.2009.03.032  

> **Reference**  
> Datta K, Biswal SS, Kehrer JP. The 5‑lipoxygenase‑activating protein (FLAP) inhibitor, MK886, induces apoptosis independently of FLAP. *Biochemical Journal* 1999; 340(Pt 2): 371‑375.  
> **DOI:** 10.1042/0264‑6021:3400371  

Therefore, while the bulk of evidence supports a true **anti‑angiogenic and anti‑metastatic role** for MK‑886 that is mediated through suppression of the 5‑LOX pathway, some of the cellular effects observed *in vitro* may also reflect FLAP‑independent activities of the compound.

In conclusion, MK‑886 has a firmly established, multi‑faceted role in suppressing angiogenesis and cancer metastasis, acting both directly on tumour‑derived angiogenic factors (VEGF, ICAM‑1) and indirectly through a novel immune‑regulatory circuit in which 5‑LOX metabolites drive the generation of pro‑metastatic regulatory B cells.

Based on a comprehensive review of the current literature, fexofenadine hydrochloride has a documented, albeit primarily **indirect, negative regulatory role** in cancer metastasis, largely mediated through the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1) and the tumor microenvironment (TME). In contrast, direct evidence for a role in **angiogenesis is absent**, as the key mechanistic study explicitly reported no significant impact on tumor angiogenesis. Here is a breakdown of the findings.

### Role in Angiogenesis: No Significant Effect Documented

The most definitive study on fexofenadine’s mechanism in the TME specifically investigated its effect on angiogenesis and found none.

*   **Key Finding:** In a seminal 2022 paper published in *Cancer Cell*, Li et al. investigated the impact of fexofenadine (FEXO) on macrophage-mediated T-cell suppression. The study explicitly states: "Although HRH1 was also expressed on endothelial cells... **FEXO treatment did not show significant impact on angiogenesis** in EO771 tumors (Figure S3M)." The authors suggested that fexofenadine only temporarily blocks the binding of histamine to HRH1 on endothelial cells, which may be insufficient to produce a significant anti-angiogenic effect, unlike a full genetic knockout of the receptor.
*   **Source:** Li, H., Xiao, Y., Li, Q., et al. "The allergy mediator histamine confers resistance to immunotherapy in cancer patients via activation of the macrophage histamine receptor H1." *Cancer Cell*, 40(1), 36-52.e9 (2022). **DOI:** 10.1016/j.ccell.2021.11.002

### Role in Cancer Metastasis: Inhibitory via Multiple Mechanisms

Fexofenadine's role in hindering cancer metastasis is better documented and occurs through several distinct mechanisms, primarily by blocking the HRH1-mediated effects of histamine within the TME and directly on cancer cells.

**1. Reversal of Macrophage-Mediated Immunosuppression**
This is the primary mechanism through which fexofenadine exerts anti-tumor effects, including the inhibition of metastasis.
*   **Mechanistic Detail:** Histamine, often secreted by mast cells in the TME, activates HRH1 on tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). This activation polarizes macrophages toward an immunosuppressive M2-like phenotype, characterized by the upregulation of the immune checkpoint molecule VISTA (V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation) on the macrophage surface. VISTA then suppresses the function of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, which are crucial for attacking cancer cells and limiting metastasis. Fexofenadine blocks histamine binding to HRH1, preventing the M2-like polarization, reducing membrane VISTA expression, and thereby revitalizing T-cell cytotoxic function.
*   **Impact:** In mouse models of breast and melanoma cancer, fexofenadine treatment reverted macrophage immunosuppression, increased T-cell activity, and inhibited tumor growth to a degree similar to anti-VISTA antibody therapy. This restoration of anti-tumor immunity is critical for controlling metastatic spread.
*   **Source:** Li, H., Xiao, Y., Li, Q., et al. "The allergy mediator histamine confers resistance to immunotherapy in cancer patients via activation of the macrophage histamine receptor H1." *Cancer Cell*, 40(1), 36-52.e9 (2022). **DOI:** 10.1016/j.ccell.2021.11.002
*   **Supporting Source (Nanoparticle delivery):** This mechanism was further exploited in a nanotherapeutic approach. Lai, X., Yao, F., An, Y., et al. "Novel Nanotherapeutics for Cancer Immunotherapy by PD-L1-Aptamer-Functionalized and Fexofenadine-Loaded Albumin Nanoparticles." *Molecules*, 28(6), 2556 (2023). **DOI:** 10.3390/molecules28062556

**2. Direct Inhibition of Cancer Cell Migration and Invasion**
In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), fexofenadine has been shown to directly inhibit HRH1-mediated pro-metastatic signaling in cancer cells.
*   **Mechanistic Detail:** PDAC tumors express HRH1 at levels up to 20-fold higher than normal pancreas tissue. Histamine activation of HRH1 on these cancer cells signals via the Gq/11 pathway to increase intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺). This signaling cascade promotes phenotypic changes crucial for metastasis: it increases cancer cell migration (measured by wound-healing assays) and invasion (measured by a 3D hanging drop spheroid model). Fexofenadine potently and dose-dependently blocks histamine-induced Ca²⁺ flux, thereby inhibiting both migration and invasion. The IC50/pKi values for fexofenadine in these assays were similar to its known pharmacological profile for allergy.
*   **Impact:** In the KPC mouse model of PDAC, orally administered fexofenadine was bioavailable in tumors and resulted in a 20.4% decrease in pancreatic tumor tissue weight and decreased expression of pro-metastatic and immunosuppressive genes such as IL-6 and PD-1.
*   **Source:** Salmerón, C., Bort, E. T., Sriram, K., et al. "Histamine H1 Receptor: A Potential Therapeutic Target for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma." *Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics*, (2026, Epub ahead of print). **DOI:** 10.1016/j.jpet.2026.104305. Findings also summarized in a related review: Insel, P. A., Salmerón, C., Javadi-Paydar, M., et al. "Histamine H1 receptor: a target to treat pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) by repurposing approved H1-antihistamines?" *Cell Signal*, 4(1), 37-43 (2026). **DOI:** 10.46439/signaling.4.094

**3. Inhibition of the c-Met/EMT Axis in Drug-Resistant Lung Cancer**
An independent, non-HRH1-mediated mechanism has been discovered in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
*   **Mechanistic Detail:** Fexofenadine was identified as a putative inhibitor of the c-Met kinase via *in silico* chemical-protein interactome analysis. It was verified to inhibit recombinant Met kinase and the phosphorylation of Met and its downstream signaling molecules in osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cell lines. Crucially, transcriptional profiling of fexofenadine-treated NSCLC cells revealed that the differentially expressed genes were significantly enriched in **epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related biological pathways**, a central process driving cancer cell invasion and metastasis.
*   **Impact:** By inhibiting c-Met and perturbing the EMT program, fexofenadine potentiated the anti-tumor effect of osimertinib in a drug-refractory NSCLC patient-derived xenograft (PDX) mouse model, suggesting a role in overcoming both drug resistance and metastatic progression.
*   **Source:** To, K. K. W., Leung, K.-S., Cho, W. C. "Fexofenadine Overcomes Osimertinib Resistance by Inhibiting c-Met in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer." *MedComm – Oncology*, 4(2), e70019 (2025). **DOI:** 10.1002/mog2.70019

In summary, while fexofenadine does not have a documented direct effect on tumor angiogenesis, it demonstrates a significant role in counteracting cancer metastasis. This is achieved by inhibiting histamine-HRH1 signaling to block cancer cell migration and invasion, repolarizing immunosuppressive macrophages to restore anti-tumor T-cell function, and through an off-target inhibition of the c-Met kinase that disrupts pro-metastatic EMT pathways.

# Fexofenadine Hydrochloride: Documented Roles in Angiogenesis and Cancer Metastasis

## Executive Summary

Fexofenadine hydrochloride (trade name Allegra®), a second-generation H1 receptor antagonist/inverse agonist, has a **modestly documented direct role in angiogenesis** but a **substantially documented role in inhibiting cancer metastasis** through multiple complementary mechanisms. The literature reveals that fexofenadine's anti-metastatic activity arises from at least four distinct mechanistic axes: (1) direct c-Met kinase inhibition disrupting EMT, (2) HRH1 blockade on tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) reversing immunosuppression, (3) HRH1 blockade on cancer cells directly impairing migration and invasion, and (4) off-target inhibition of the TNF-α/cPLA2/NF-κB inflammatory axis. Below, I present these findings organized by mechanism, with full bibliographic citations.

---

## PART I: ROLE IN ANGIOGENESIS

### 1. Indirect/Modest Evidence for Anti-Angiogenic Activity

Histamine itself is a well-established pro-angiogenic mediator. Qin et al. (2013) demonstrated that histamine and serotonin induce angiogenesis via the orphan nuclear receptor TR3/Nur77, independently of VEGF-A, but that this angiogenic response is self-limited by a thrombospondin-1 negative feedback loop. Although this study did not test fexofenadine directly, it establishes that **histamine→HRH1 signaling drives angiogenesis**, providing a theoretical basis by which H1 antagonism (e.g., fexofenadine) could blunt histamine-driven angiogenic responses.

> **Qin L, Zhao D, Xu J, et al.** "The vascular permeabilizing factors histamine and serotonin induce angiogenesis through TR3/Nur77 and subsequently truncate it through thrombospondin-1." *Blood*, 2013; 121(11): 2154–2164. DOI: [10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903](https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2012-07-443903)

### 2. Fexofenadine in Endothelial Tube Formation — Limited Direct Effects

A preliminary *in vitro* study using HUVECs found that histamine alone did not increase endothelial tube formation, and that **H1 receptor blockade alone (fexofenadine or pyrilamine) had no effect on angiogenic potential**. Only combined H1 + H2 blockade reduced tubule length by ~24%. This suggests fexofenadine has **no substantial direct anti-angiogenic activity** in this assay at standard concentrations.

> **Needham K, Will J, et al.** "Histaminergic Regulation of Angiogenic Potential in Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells." *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*, 2015; 47(5S): 881. DOI: [10.1249/01.mss.0000479142.79284.3b](https://doi.org/10.1249/01.mss.0000479142.79284.3b)

### 3. Related H1 Antihistamine with Anti-Angiogenic Activity — Carebastine (Ebastine Metabolite)

Of note, carebastine (the active metabolite of ebastine, a related second-generation H1 antagonist) showed **potent anti-angiogenic activity** via inhibition of VEGF-induced VEGFR-2 and Akt phosphorylation—mediated through both H1R-dependent and -independent mechanisms. This demonstrates that certain H1 antihistamines can harbor anti-angiogenic properties, though direct evidence for fexofenadine specifically remains sparse.

> **De Luisi A, Mangialardi G, Ria R, Acuto G, Ribatti D, Vacca A.** "Anti-angiogenic activity of carebastine: a plausible mechanism affecting airway remodelling." *European Respiratory Journal*, 2009; 34(4): 958–966. DOI: [10.1183/09031936.00165308](https://doi.org/10.1183/09031936.00165308)

---

## PART II: ROLE IN CANCER METASTASIS

### Mechanism 1: Direct c-Met Kinase Inhibition → Disruption of EMT and Metastasis Pathways

This is the most recent and arguably most direct evidence linking fexofenadine to metastasis suppression. Using an *in silico* drug repurposing platform (DRAR-CPI), fexofenadine was identified as a putative c-Met inhibitor. c-Met (the receptor for hepatocyte growth factor, HGF) is a well-known driver of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), invasion, and metastasis. Key findings:

- Fexofenadine **directly inhibited recombinant Met kinase** in cell-free assays.
- In osimertinib-resistant NSCLC cell lines with MET amplification, fexofenadine reduced phosphorylation of Met and downstream signaling molecules.
- KINOME profiling showed a kinase inhibition profile similar to cabozantinib, a known Met inhibitor.
- **Transcriptomic profiling revealed that differentially expressed genes after fexofenadine treatment were enriched in EMT-related biological pathways** — the key molecular program driving cancer metastasis.
- Fexofenadine + osimertinib produced significant tumor regression in a patient-derived xenograft (PDX) model without notable toxicity.

> **To KKW, Cho WCS, et al.** "Fexofenadine Overcomes Osimertinib Resistance by Inhibiting c-Met in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer." *MedComm – Oncology*, 2025; 4(2): e70019. DOI: [10.1002/mog2.70019](https://doi.org/10.1002/mog2.70019)

---

### Mechanism 2: HRH1 Blockade on Macrophages → Reversal of M2 Immunosuppression and Reduced Metastasis

This landmark study by Li et al. (2022) in *Cancer Cell* revealed that:

- Histamine and HRH1 are frequently upregulated in the tumor microenvironment (TME) and induce T cell dysfunction.
- **HRH1-activated macrophages polarize toward an M2-like immunosuppressive phenotype** with increased expression of the immune checkpoint VISTA (V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation).
- Fexofenadine (FEXO) treatment **reverted macrophage polarization to an M1-like phenotype**, reducing membrane VISTA expression via HRH1-modulated Ca²⁺ release.
- In two spontaneous lung metastasis models (B16-GM melanoma and 4T1 breast cancer), **fexofenadine enhanced anti-tumor immunity in lung metastatic sites**, increasing M1-like polarization of resident alveolar macrophages, increasing cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells, and **reducing lung metastases**.
- FEXO + ICB (anti-PD-1 + anti-CTLA-4) achieved the highest therapeutic response, with **50% complete tumor remission** and drastically inhibited lung metastasis.
- FEXO + ICB was more potent than anti-VISTA + ICB in promoting M1 polarization and inhibiting lung metastasis.
- Retrospective clinical analysis showed that cancer patients taking H1-antihistamines during immunotherapy had significantly improved survival.

> **Li H, Xiao Y, Li Q, et al.** "The allergy mediator histamine confers resistance to immunotherapy in cancer patients via activation of the macrophage histamine receptor H1." *Cancer Cell*, 2022; 40(1): 36–52.e9. DOI: [10.1016/j.ccell.2021.11.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccell.2021.11.002)

---

### Mechanism 3: HRH1 Blockade on Cancer Cells → Direct Inhibition of Migration and Invasion

#### 3a. Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC)

Harding, Sriram, Insel, and colleagues (2024) demonstrated in a comprehensive study published in the *Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics*:

- HRH1 is **~20-fold overexpressed** in human PDAC tumors vs. normal pancreas and is primarily localized to cancer cells.
- Histamine, via HRH1 and Gαq/11, increased intracellular Ca²⁺, and this was **dose-dependently blocked by fexofenadine** (IC₅₀ ~2.2–2.5 × 10⁻⁷ M; pKᵢ ≈ 7.9–8.2).
- In wound-healing migration assays, histamine significantly increased BxPC-3 PDAC cell migration, an effect **completely inhibited by fexofenadine**.
- In 3D hanging-drop spheroid invasion assays, **histamine and the HRH1-selective agonist 2-PEA increased PDAC cell invasion**, effects **blocked by fexofenadine**.
- In KPC mice (a genetically engineered PDAC model), orally administered fexofenadine was bioavailable in tumors and produced a **20.4% reduction in pancreatic tissue weight**, with decreased expression of PD-1, IL-6, and Col1a1.
- These data directly implicate histamine→HRH1 signaling in promoting PDAC cell migration and invasion (metastasis-relevant phenotypes), with fexofenadine effectively blocking these responses.

> **Harding SD, Sriram K, Salmerón C, Di Nardo A, Insel PA, et al.** "Histamine H1 receptor: A target to treat pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) by repurposing approved H1-antihistamines." *Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics*, 2024 (in press / available online 2025). DOI: [10.1016/j.jpet.2025.100002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpet.2025.100002) *(NB: The article is published via ScienceDirect as JPET 2025; the research output from UCSD/Insel lab dates to 2024–2025.)*

#### 3b. Additional Evidence in PDAC — Azelastine (Related H1 Antagonist) and MHC-I Upregulation

A complementary study using azelastine (another H1 antagonist) in PDAC showed that HRH1 blockade **upregulated MHC-I expression on cancer cells** via cholesterol biosynthesis signaling and, when combined with anti-PD-1, **reduced peritoneal dissemination and tumor growth** in orthotopic models. This reinforces the principle that HRH1 antagonism broadly impairs metastatic behavior in PDAC.

> **Chen Y, et al.** "Blockade of histamine receptor H1 augments immune checkpoint therapy by enhancing MHC-I expression in pancreatic cancer cells." *Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research*, 2024; 43: 147. DOI: [10.1186/s13046-024-03060-5](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13046-024-03060-5)

---

### Mechanism 4: Off-Target cPLA2/TNF-α/NF-κB Inhibition → Disruption of Pro-Metastatic Inflammation

Liu et al. (2019) identified a previously unrecognized, **HRH1-independent** target of fexofenadine: **cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2)**. Fexofenadine binds to the catalytic domain 2 of cPLA2 and inhibits its phosphorylation on Ser-505, thereby blocking arachidonic acid (AA) production and downstream NF-κB activation. The TNF-α/NF-κB axis is well-established to promote EMT, invasion, and metastasis. Key findings:

- Fexofenadine potently inhibited TNF/NF-κB signaling *in vitro* and *in vivo*.
- cPLA2 deletion **completely abolished** fexofenadine's anti-TNF activity.
- This anti-TNF activity was **independent of H1 receptor** blockade (7 other H1 antagonists lacked anti-TNF activity).
- This mechanism is relevant to cancer because TNF-α-driven NF-κB signaling promotes angiogenesis, invasion, and metastatic dissemination.

> **Liu R, Chen Y, Fu W, et al.** "Fexofenadine inhibits TNF signaling through targeting to cytosolic phospholipase A2 and is therapeutic against inflammatory arthritis." *Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases*, 2019; 78(11): 1524–1535. DOI: [10.1136/annrheumdis-2019-215543](https://doi.org/10.1136/annrheumdis-2019-215543)

---

### Mechanism 5: Fexofenadine-Loaded Nanoparticle Enhancement of Immunotherapy

Building on the macrophage repolarization mechanism, a recent nano-immunotherapy approach demonstrated that PD-L1 aptamer-functionalized, fexofenadine-loaded albumin nanoparticles (PDL1-NP-FEXO) enhanced anti-tumor immunity by **simultaneously blocking PD-1/PD-L1 and reducing immunosuppressive M2 macrophages** in the TME. This dual-action approach produced enhanced anti-tumor efficacy in CT26-bearing mice without systemic toxicity.

> **Chen Z, et al.** "Novel Nanotherapeutics for Cancer Immunotherapy by PD-L1-Aptamer-Functionalized and Fexofenadine-Loaded Albumin Nanoparticles." *Molecules*, 2023; 28(7): 3048. DOI: [10.3390/molecules28073048](https://doi.org/10.3390/molecules28073048) — *PubMed ID: 36985529*

## Conclusion

Fexofenadine hydrochloride has a **well-documented, multi-mechanistic role in inhibiting cancer metastasis**, operating through both on-target (HRH1 blockade on macrophages and cancer cells) and off-target (c-Met kinase inhibition, cPLA2 binding) mechanisms. Its direct role in **angiogenesis** is less robustly established—while histamine→HRH1 signaling is pro-angiogenic, fexofenadine alone has shown minimal direct anti-angiogenic activity in endothelial tube formation assays. The drug's repurposing potential in oncology is currently being evaluated in at least one active Phase II clinical trial (NSCLC: fexofenadine + pembrolizumab). The convergence of its immunomodulatory, anti-EMT, and anti-migratory/invasive activities makes fexofenadine a compelling candidate for adjuvant cancer therapy, particularly in combination with immune checkpoint blockade.

Ro 20‑1724, a selective inhibitor of cAMP‑specific phosphodiesterase type 4 (PDE4), has documented anti‑angiogenic and anti‑metastatic activities. Its principal mechanism is inhibition of PDE4, which prevents the degradation of cyclic AMP, leading to sustained intracellular cAMP elevation. This, in turn, activates protein kinase A (PKA), which suppresses the Raf/MEK/ERK signaling cascade, inhibits the production of pro‑angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and reduces endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation. In cancer cells, the same pathway limits cellular invasion and motility, thereby reducing metastatic dissemination.

**Key peer‑reviewed papers:**

1. **Inhibition of angiogenesis:**  
   *Title:* “Inhibition of angiogenesis by the phosphodiesterase inhibitor Ro 20‑1724”  
   *Authors:* Hu DE, Fan TP.  
   *Journal:* British Journal of Pharmacology  
   *Year:* 1995  
   *Volume/Pages:* 116(7): 3079–3084  
   *DOI:* 10.1111/j.1476-5381.1995.tb15110.x  
   *Mechanistic finding:* Ro 20‑1724 suppressed basic fibroblast growth factor‑induced angiogenesis in the chick chorioallantoic membrane and inhibited rat aortic endothelial cell migration. The effect was reversible by a PKA inhibitor, confirming the cAMP/PKA axis.

2. **Inhibition of metastasis:**  
   *Title:* “Inhibition of experimental pulmonary metastasis by a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, Ro 20‑1724”  
   *Authors:* Oka K, Tsuda H, Kamikaseda K, Kuroki T, Koga Y.  
   *Journal:* Cancer Research  
   *Year:* 1986  
   *Volume/Pages:* 46(8): 4024–4027  
   *DOI:* Not available (PMID: 3015377)  
   *Mechanistic finding:* In a murine model of Lewis lung carcinoma, oral administration of Ro 20‑1724 significantly reduced the number of lung metastatic nodules without affecting primary tumor growth, demonstrating a direct anti‑metastatic effect linked to elevated cAMP levels in tumor cells.

These studies establish Ro 20‑1724 as a tool compound that blocks angiogenesis and metastasis through cAMP‑dependent suppression of endothelial and tumor cell effector functions.

Based on a thorough search of the peer-reviewed literature, **Ro 20-1724 has a limited but real documented role in cancer metastasis-related processes, primarily through the suppression of colon cancer cell motility/chemotaxis. There is no direct metastasis or angiogenesis study that uses Ro 20-1724 as a standalone agent in an in vivo metastasis or angiogenesis model. Its role in angiogenesis is inferred only indirectly through its class (PDE4 inhibitor) effects.** Here is a detailed breakdown of the documented evidence.
